SUBJECT DESCRIPTION
Machine Learning (ML) is a core pillar of modern data analytics and artificial
intelligence. Its capacity to extract patterns from data, construct predictive models,
and support complex decision-making has made it an essential competency for
any professional working at the intersection of data and business. From demand
1
forecasting and customer segmentation to fraud detection and natural language
processing, ML techniques are reshaping how organizations operate, compete,
and create value.
This course provides a rigorous and systematic introduction to Machine Learning,
designed for students in Data and Business Analytics who seek both a solid
theoretical foundation and the practical skills to build, evaluate, and critically
assess ML systems. The course spans the full ML workflow: from data curation
and feature engineering, through supervised and unsupervised learning, to deep
learning architectures and their business applications. Reinforcement learning is
introduced as a conceptual framework for sequential decision-making.
The course is structured around lectures, guided coding notebooks, two
substantial take-home assignments, and a group project. Lectures develop
conceptual and mathematical understanding. Notebooks demonstrate how theory
translates into working code, using real datasets. Take-home assignments require
students to independently build complete ML pipelines under realistic constraints.
The group project requires teams to identify and address a significant, original
problem using ML methods appropriate to its complexity.
Students completing this course will be equipped to work effectively in data
science and analytics roles that require ML competency, to communicate ML
results to technical and non-technical audiences, and to evaluate the
appropriateness, quality, and limitations of ML solutions deployed in organizational
contexts.

research, code documentation, code generation, and code fixing with appropriate
acknowledgement. GenAI may not be used for exams, writing conclusions, or
extracting insights for the assignments. If a student is found to have used AI-
generated content inappropriately, it will be considered academic misconduct, and
the student might fail the respective assignment or the course.
If you are unsure whether you are using GenAI tools appropriately in this course, I

PROGRAM
SESSION 1 (LIVE IN-PERSON)
Course Introduction
In this session we will review the course logistics and organization together with basic
concepts and requirements along the subject.
SESSION 2 (LIVE IN-PERSON)
Introduction to Machine Learning
In this session, we will start learning about the meaning of machine learning and its objectives.
We’ll see some examples of learning models. Finally, we’ll do some python exercises to
review basic concepts of the programming language.
SESSION 3 (LIVE IN-PERSON)
Types of learning
In this session we will review the different types of learning in ML and their applications. We'll
face the first practical exercise of the course.
SESSION 4 (LIVE IN-PERSON)
Supervised Learning - Regression
SESSION 5 (LIVE IN-PERSON)
Supervised Learning - Classification
In this session we will introduce some classification models such as Logistic Regression or
Generative models. We will compare different classification models. Finally, we will do some
related exercises.
5
SESSION 6 (LIVE IN-PERSON)
Overfitting and Regularization techniques
This session focuses on understanding overfitting as a key challenge in machine
learning—where models capture noise and perform poorly on unseen data—and
explores regularization techniques as a solution. It covers how methods like L1
and L2 introduce penalties to control model complexity, helping achieve a better
balance between bias and variance and improving generalization performance.
SESSION 7 (LIVE IN-PERSON)
Practical Session - Supervised Learning
SESSION 8 (LIVE IN-PERSON)
Tree-Based methods
In this session we will see the basics of decision trees and their related ensemble
methods: bagging and boosting.
SESSION 9 (LIVE IN-PERSON)
Practical Session - Trees
The idea of this session is to learn how to apply the tree-based methods to solve real
problems. Essentially, we will put in practice the Random Forest and XGBoost algorithms.
SESSION 10 (LIVE IN-PERSON)
Group work introduction
SESSION 11 (LIVE IN-PERSON)

Transformers I
This session introduces
as a foundational deep learning
Transformers
architecture that revolutionized AI by using self-attention mechanisms to model
relationships within sequential data. It explains how transformers process entire
inputs in parallel and leverage encoder–decoder structures and attention layers to
capture long-range dependencies, enabling state-of-the-art performance in tasks
such as language modeling, translation, and generative AI.

Retrieval Augmented Generation
This session introduces
as a key
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
approach in Generative AI that enhances large language models by combining
information retrieval with text generation. It explains how RAG systems retrieve
relevant data from external knowledge sources and use it to augment the model’s
input, enabling more accurate, up-to-date, and context-aware responses while
reducing hallucinations and improving reliability.
SESSION 27 (LIVE IN-PERSON)
Group presentations I
First of three sessions dedicated to final group project presentations. Each group

analysis, and depth of understanding demonstrated under questioning. Groups are
expected to present a complete, original ML project addressing a real-world
problem of non-trivial complexity.

criteria as session 27.

EVALUATION CRITERIA
Disclaimer: The assessment method may be subject to modifications. Should
changes occur, students will be notified on the first day of class and provided with
a written document detailing the modifications.
The evaluation scheme for this course reflects its pedagogical design: the majority
of the grade is determined by sustained, independent work carried out over the full
duration of the semester, rather than by performance in a single terminal
assessment.
Class Participation [15%] Active participation is expected throughout the
course. Evaluation is based on the quality and not the frequency of
contributions to in-class discussion. A high-quality contribution demonstrates
engagement with the material, critical reasoning, and the capacity to connect
concepts across sessions. Attendance is a prerequisite for participation and
is tracked; students who do not meet the university's attendance
requirements will be evaluated accordingly under the institutional policy.
Students are encouraged to ask questions, challenge assumptions, and
engage with the work of their peers. The following types of participation do
not contribute positively to the evaluation: contributions that merely restate
what has already been said, interventions that are off-topic or that reflect
inattention, and questions that arise from failure to engage with the course
material outside of class.
Take-home Assignments [30%]: Several substantial take-home
assignments are distributed across the semester. Each assignment has a
deadline. Assignments submitted after the deadline will receive a grade of
zero without exception. All assignments are individual work. A structured
review session is dedicated to each assignment following the submission
deadline, focusing on the most consequential errors observed across
submissions. Attendance at review sessions is strongly recommended. The

conclusions. Failure to acknowledge the use of GenAI will be treated as
academic misconduct. Use of GenAI with appropriate acknowledgement will
not affect the grade.
Group Project and Presentation [20%]: Groups of up to five students
develop an original ML project across the second half of the semester. The
project must address a problem of genuine complexity using methods
appropriate to the task. Replication of existing tutorials or minor extensions
of standard benchmark exercises are not acceptable. Groups are expected
to make and defend non-trivial methodological choices and to produce
results that reflect a serious engagement with the problem.
Quiz (Final) [35%]: An in-class quiz administered at session 30, covering all
material from sessions 1 through 29. The quiz is closed-book. It is designed
to assess cumulative understanding of the full course, including deep
learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning.

SUBJECT DESCRIPTION
Macroeconomics is the branch of economics that studies the behavior of the
economy as a whole, treating it as a single aggregate. It seeks to identify the
factors that make a country's economy dynamic and healthy, as well as those that
explain the difficulties and instability sometimes experienced by others. A healthy
economy can be characterized by steady economic growth, full employment, low
and stable inflation, sound public finances, and a balanced external sector.
Macroeconomics helps us understand, prevent, and counteract the causes of low
growth, high unemployment, pronounced business cycle fluctuations, and
imbalances in the public and external sectors. Understanding these issues
provides the foundation for analyzing the potential role of governments in
improving economic performance through public policy, as well as for assessing
the possible consequences of inadequate macroeconomic policies.
Prevailing and expected aggregate economic conditions are key considerations in
business decision-making. A favorable macroeconomic environment is a
prerequisite for the success of entrepreneurial projects and for achieving
reasonable returns on financial investments. This course provides students with
the fundamental tools needed to understand real-world economic developments
and their implications for business activity. It also aims to develop students' ability
to critically assess economic conditions and macroeconomic policies.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES
2
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to analyze and
interpret current economic developments, assess the overall state of an economy,
identify the factors underlying strong or weak economic performance, and critically
evaluate the macroeconomic policies in place, which are often the subject of
significant debate.
To achieve these objectives, the course develops a theoretical framework that
explains the relationships among the main macroeconomic aggregates. Particular
emphasis is placed on the practical implications of the underlying theory. The
analytical treatment of core models is kept as simple and intuitive as possible,
relying primarily on graphical analysis.
Within economic science, Macroeconomics remains one of the most debated
fields, particularly with regard to the choice of a single theoretical framework
capable of explaining real-world events. Students are introduced to the main
schools of thought and encouraged to assess the practical relevance and
limitations of different theoretical approaches.
Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) issues-both public and corporate-
are incorporated into class discussions on economic performance and the role of
governments in economic life. Students are encouraged to identify sustainability-
related challenges, apply economic tools to analyze them, and use economic
reasoning to evaluate appropriate policy responses.

SUBJECT DESCRIPTION
Every data analysis a business analyst performs, from a pandas transformation or
a scikit-learn model to a Monte Carlo simulation, runs on an operating system and,
increasingly, on parallel hardware. This hardware may include multicore
processors, multiprocessor servers, computing clusters, and GPU accelerators.
Understanding these systems helps analysts explain why one workload runs in
seconds while a slightly larger one takes hours, why adding processors can slow a
program, and when moving a workload to a cluster or GPU is worth the additional
complexity.
This course builds that understanding through theory and Python examples in data
management and analysis. The first half focuses on operating systems. Students
study processes, threads, memory, storage, and input/output, and how these
resources affect analytical workloads. They also learn to work in a Unix/Linux
environment using the terminal, the standard environment for servers, clusters,
and cloud computing. Using standard tools, students observe running programs
and diagnose common performance problems, such as insufficient memory, slow
input/output, and competition for processor resources.
The second half focuses on parallel computing. Students study the architecture of
modern parallel systems, including multicore processors, shared-memory and
distributed-memory systems, computing clusters, and GPU accelerators. They
then use Python tools from the data analytics ecosystem to implement and
evaluate parallel workloads. These tools include threading and multiprocessing,
,
, NumPy vectorization, Dask for partitioned and
concurrent.futures joblib
distributed data processing, and CuPy for GPU computing.
Students also develop a practical framework for evaluating performance. They
study execution time, speedup, efficiency, overhead, Amdahl's Law, and strong
and weak scaling. Rather than treating these concepts as theory only, students
test them by measuring their own programs, validating their results, and explaining
why performance does or does not improve.
Practical work is conducted on students' laptops and on the University's high-
performance computing cluster. The course culminates in a group project in which
students select a realistic analytics workload, establish a correct sequential
baseline, develop a parallel implementation, run it on the cluster, measure its
scaling behavior, and explain the technical and practical significance of the results.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES
The objective of this course is to provide students with a practical understanding of
operating systems and parallel computing for data analysis and management. The
course covers operating-system roles and structure, processes and threads, CPU
scheduling, memory, storage, input/output, Linux command-line tools,
2
concurrency, parallel architectures, parallel programming in Python, performance
and scalability, distributed data processing, and GPU computing.
At the end of the course, students should be able to:
Explain the role and principal components of a modern operating system and
how they affect the execution and performance of data-analysis workloads.
Work in a Linux environment by navigating the file system, managing files
and permissions, combining commands, automating simple tasks, and
inspecting running processes and resource usage.
Use standard operating-system tools to identify and diagnose common
performance problems, including insufficient memory, input/output
bottlenecks, and competition for processor resources.
Differentiate between concurrency and parallelism, determine whether a
workload is primarily CPU- or input/output-bound, and select an appropriate
execution strategy.
Describe the architecture of modern parallel systems, including multicore
processors, shared-memory and distributed-memory systems, computing
clusters, and GPU accelerators, and explain how these architectures affect
program performance.
Transform a correct sequential data-analysis program into a parallel
implementation using appropriate Python tools, including multiprocessing,
concurrent.futures, joblib, NumPy, Dask, and CuPy.
Validate that sequential and parallel implementations produce equivalent
results and identify errors caused by decomposition, shared state, task
ordering, or nondeterministic execution.
Measure and analyze the performance of parallel programs by computing
speedup, efficiency, and overhead, applying Amdahl's Law, and
distinguishing between strong and weak scaling.

SUBJECT DESCRIPTION
This course offers an introduction to Organizational Behavior, a field on human
differences, emotions, perceptions, behaviors, and interactions within the context
of work organizations. More specifically, the topics include personality, attitude,
emotion, and motivation at the individual level, as well as leadership,
communication, and conflict at the group/team level. This course addresses issues
such as understanding individual differences, motivating employees with various
needs, leading groups and teams, resolving conflicts in an organizational context
and, eventually, building a high-growth and sustainable organization where people
will flourish.

LEARNING OBJECTIVES
- Become a more confident, dynamic, and persuasive presenter.
Participants with successful completion of this course should achieve the following
objectives:
1.
Raise awareness and sensitivity regarding the impact of human-related issues in the
workplace.
2.
List basic organizational behavior principles and explain how these principles
influence human behavior in the workplace.
3.
Analyze individual human behavior by using knowledge of personality, attitudes,
emotions, and motivations.
4.
Understand group behavior elements, such as leadership, power, politics,
communication, conflict, and negotiation.
5.
Enhance critical thinking skills through case studies, class discussions, and group
projects.

SUBJECT DESCRIPTION
1
“Strategy is a plan, a method, a series of actions designed to achieve a specific
goal or effect”
(Wordsmyth Dictionary)
This course aims to assist you in becoming an effective and responsible strategist,
able to critically evaluate existing strategies of firms, and make well-grounded
recommendations directing the future of organizations.
We will start by examining reasons why some firms outperform other firms—one of
the most fundamental questions in the field of strategy. We systematically examine
what drives profitability differences across industries and how firms can effectively
adapt strategy to their industry. We then explore how firms can distinguish
themselves from competitors within their industry and create a competitive
advantage. You will learn key tools and frameworks to navigate a firm’s corporate
strategy—where to compete?—and business strategy—how to compete?
In the second half of the course will focus on strategizing in increasingly dynamic
and unpredictable environments. We will learn how to incorporate potential moves
from competitors, artificial intelligence, and sustainability goals in a firm’s strategy
and current challenges in developing an effective, timely, and responsible strategy.

SUBJECT DESCRIPTION
1
Time series analysis comprises the methods used to analyse data indexed in time
in order to extract meaningful statistics, identify structure, and produce forecasts.
Time series analysis and forecasting are among the most widely applied data
science techniques in business, finance, engineering and logistics. Examples of
time series include the continuous monitoring of a person's heart rate, hourly
readings of air temperature, the daily closing price of a company's stock, monthly
rainfall, and yearly sales figures. The field has a well-established theoretical
grounding in statistics and dynamic systems theory.
This course introduces the most important methods used to model time series
data: decomposition, exponential smoothing and ARIMA models. All practical work
is carried out in R, using the tidyverts family of packages (tsibble, feasts, fable).
The course is taught as an applied engagement rather than a lecture series.
Students work in teams of three to four, and each team is assigned one real
business case at the start of the term. That case becomes their running problem
for the whole semester: every technique introduced in class is immediately applied
to it, evaluated on its merits, and either adopted or rejected with a documented
justification.
PREREQUISITES FOR TAKING THIS SUBJECT:
Fundamentals of Probability and Statistics.
Fundamentals of Data Analysis.
Programming and Data Visualisation

LEARNING OBJECTIVES
The main objective of this course is to provide students with a working
methodology and a solid knowledge of the use of time series analysis in business.
At the end of the course, students should be able to:
Differentiate statistical models for independent observations from models for
observations with temporal correlation.
Identify patterns in correlated data: trend, seasonality and cycles.
Understand and model time series data with exponential smoothing (ETS)
and ARIMA models.
Understand and apply the most important algorithms in the field.
Design an appropriate methodology for each type of time series data
(financial, hierarchical, seasonal, intermittent, multiple-seasonal).
2
Use the standard diagnostic toolkit: ACF, PACF, CCF, stationarity tests,
residual diagnostics and out-of-sample accuracy measures.
Formulate a forecasting problem from an incomplete business brief, and
defend a recommendation that is technically sound, properly validated and
useful for the decision it serves.

TEACHING METHODOLOGY
The emphasis is on methods that are replicable and testable, and on practical
examples. Sessions follow a fixed three-block structure:
30 minutes. Concept and R application. A focused treatment of the
technique of the week, oriented around what problem it solves, followed
immediately by worked examples in R on a shared dataset.
30 minutes. Business Case Lab. Each team applies the technique to its
own assigned case. Working code is not the requirement; progress is. A
valid output may be a plot, a methodological decision, a hypothesis, a data
transformation, a fitted model, or an evidenced argument for why the
technique does not apply to their case.
20 minutes. Case Clinic. Selected teams present what they attempted,
what they found and where they are blocked. The rest of the class
challenges the reasoning, and the professor closes with feedback.
The classroom therefore functions as a laboratory: the substantive work on each
case happens in class, with the professor present, rather than being deferred to
homework. Because several teams work on each case, students see the same
technique behave differently across comparable business problems. Each team
maintains a decision log throughout the term, recording every assumption, data
source, method tested and decision taken, with its justification. The log is the raw
material of the final report.

BUSINESS CASES
The cases used in this course span different industries, data frequencies, decision
horizons and failure modes, so that the same methodological syllabus produces
four genuinely different analytical problems.
CASE 1. HAPPY COW ICE CREAM (retail and FMCG) Asia Case Research
Centre, The University of Hong Kong. A small vegan ice cream maker with
transaction-level point-of-sale data from a campus store. Short history,
weather- and calendar-driven demand, and a store manager who already
intervenes in the series. Forecasting problem: short-horizon demand for
replenishment and assortment decisions.
CASE 2. BALEARIC AIRLINES (airlines, revenue management). IESE
Business School. Daily demand for priority-class seats on a single Barcelona-
Palma route with a two-tier fare structure and a fixed 186-seat capacity.
Forecasting problem: setting a seat protection level two months before
departure, which requires the demand distribution rather than a point
forecast.
CASE 3. CLEAN AIR LIMITED (manufacturing, supply chain) Ivey
Publishing, Ivey Business School. Emission control systems for Indian
commercial vehicles, with imported components on six- and twelve-month
lead times committed a year in advance. Forecasting problem: an ordering
and inventory plan under a short history containing structural breaks, with
contractually asymmetric costs of error.
CASE 4. WAYFAIR (e-commerce, forecasting at scale) Foresight: The
International Journal of Applied Forecasting, 2025 Q4. A published account
of Wayfair's hierarchical forecasting engine: millions of products, monthly
demand one to eighteen months ahead, extreme sparsity and a rapidly
expanding catalogue. Forecasting problem: whether hierarchical
reconciliation and ensembling outperform forecasting each series
independently, and at what cost in complexity.

1. INTRODUCTION
Unsupervised learning techniques has grown importance over the last years:
•
1. Cancer research
2. Fake news
3. Spam filter
4. Marketing and sales
5. Fraud detection
In unsupervised learning the learning algorithm focuses solely on detecting structure in unlabeled
•
input data. One generally differentiates between:
1. Clustering, where the goal is to find homogeneous subgroups within the data; the grouping
is based on distance between observations.
2. Dimensionality reduction, where the goal is to identify patterns in the features of the data.
Dimensionality reduction is often used to facilitate visualization of the data, as well as a pre-
processing method before supervised learning.
In real world, there is generally much more supervised problems than unsupervised problems.

What is data variation? Why is it important?
Variation is a way to show how data is dispersed or spread out. It shows
•
how far apart data points are from one another.
This is important because the amount of variability determines how well
•
you can generalize results from the sample to your population.
The higher variance a machine learning model can capture the better.

1. INTRODUCTION
To a computer, an image is just a grid of numbers. A CNN learns to find patterns in that grid (edges,
•
textures, shapes) and uses them to recognize what the image shows.

•

•
eye sees.
Older methods needed filters designed by hand. A CNN learns its filters from labelled examples, so it
•
needs little pre-processing.
CNNs are behind photo search, face unlock, medical image screening, factory quality inspection and
•
driver-assistance cameras.

features contributes to the probability of any given output

2.1. ADVANTAGES OF CNNs OVER MLPs
MLPs use one perceptron for each pixel in an image and the number of weights rapidly becomes
•
unmanageable for large images. Example: a 224×224 color image has 150,528 inputs, so a single fully
connected neuron needs 150,528 weights. A 3×3 convolution filter needs only 27 weights and is reused across
the whole image.
Another common problem is that MLPs react differently to an input (images) and its shifted version — they
•
are not translation invariant. Thus, spatial information is lost when the image is flattened (matrix to vector) into
an MLP.
For example, if a dog appears in the top left of the image in one picture and the bottom right of another
•
picture, the MLP will try to correct itself and assume that a dog will always appear in this section of the image.

ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit): f(x) = max(0, x). Negative values become 0;
•

Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU)
It is usually applied after each convolution, often after batch normalization.
•
Without a non-linear function, a stack of layers behaves like one single linear
layer and cannot learn complex shapes.
Intuition: each value in a feature map says how strongly a pattern is present.
•
ReLU keeps the positive evidence and drops the negative responses.
ReLU is cheap to compute and lets deep networks train faster than older
•
functions such as sigmoid or tanh.
Not every layer uses it: the output layer uses softmax instead, and modern
•
networks often use variants such as Leaky ReLU or SiLU.

4. HYPERPARAMETERS & TRAINING
4.3. BATCH NORMALIZATION
Problem: as the weights change during training, the values passed between layers keep changing scale, which
•
slows learning down.
Batch normalization rescales a layer's outputs, for each mini-batch, to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. The
•
network then learns its own scale and shift for each channel.
What you gain:
•
1. Faster, more stable training, even for very deep networks such as ResNet
2. Higher learning rates can be used
3. Less sensitivity to how the weights are initialized
4. A mild regularization effect, often used together with dropout
35

4. HYPERPARAMETERS & TRAINING
4.3. BATCH NORMALIZATION
Batch normalization is placed after a convolution or fully connected layer and before ReLU: Conv →BatchNorm
•
→ReLU.
During training it uses the statistics of the current batch; at prediction time it uses averages stored during training.

2012: AlexNet won the ImageNet challenge (1.2M images, 1,000 classes) with 15% top-5 error, against 26% for the

•
Beyond classifying a whole image, CNNs detect objects with boxes (YOLO) and segment every pixel (U-Net).
•
Everyday uses: photo search by content, face unlock on phones, product recognition in shops, screening of X-rays
•
and skin lesions.

6. APPLICATIONS
6.2. VIDEO ANALYSIS
A video is a sequence of images, so it adds a time dimension.
•
Two common approaches: 3D convolutions that slide over space and time at once, or a 2D CNN on each frame
•
followed by a model that combines the frames.
Uses: action recognition in sports footage, traffic and crowd monitoring, and driver-assistance cameras that track
•
pedestrians and lanes.

6. APPLICATIONS
6.3. NATURAL LANGUAGE PROCESSING
Text can be treated as a 1D sequence: a filter slides over groups of 3 to 5 words and detects phrases.
•
Around 2014 to 2017, CNNs gave strong results in sentence classification and sentiment analysis (Kim, 2014).
•
Since 2018, Transformers (BERT, GPT) have replaced CNNs for most language tasks. CNNs remain useful for small,
•
fast text classifiers.

OBJECT DETECTION WITH YOLO
YOLO is an algorithm that uses neural networks to provide real-time object detection.
•
Object detection is a phenomenon in computer vision that involves the detection of various objects in digital
•
images or videos. This phenomenon seeks to answer two basic questions:
1.
What is the object? This question seeks to identify the object in a specific image.
2.
Where is it? This question seeks to establish the exact location of the object within the image.
YOLO is an abbreviation for the term ‘You Only Look Once’. This is an algorithm that detects and recognizes
•
various objects in a picture (in real-time). Object detection in YOLO is done as a regression problem and
provides the class probabilities of the detected images.
YOLO algorithm employs convolutional neural networks (CNN) and the prediction in the entire image is done
•
in a single algorithm run.
YOLO algorithm is important because of the following reasons:
•
Speed: This algorithm improves the speed of detection because it can predict objects in real-time.
•
High accuracy: YOLO is a predictive technique that provides accurate results with minimal background
•
errors.
Learning capabilities: The algorithm has excellent learning capabilities that enable it to learn the
•
representations of objects and apply them in object detection.

3. GENERATIVE MODELS
3.2. QUADRATIC DISCRIMINANT ANALYSIS
DISCUSSION
Why would one prefer LDA to QDA, or viceversa?
The answer lies in the bias-variance trade-off. When there are p predictors, then estimating a covariance matrix
requires estimating p(p+1)/2 parameters. QDA estimates a separate covariance matrix for each class, for a total of
Kp(p+1)/2 parameters. With 50 predictors this is some multiple of 1.275, which is a lot of parameters. By instead
assuming that the K classes share a common covariance matrix, the LDA model becomes linear in x, which means there
are Kp linear coefficients to estimate. Consequently, LDA is a much less flexible classifier than QDA, and so has
substantially lower variance. This can potentially lead to improved prediction performance. But there is a trade-off: if
LDA’s assumption that the K classes share a common covariance matrix is badly off, then LDA can suffer from high bias.
Roughly speaking, LDA tends to be a better bet than QDA if there are relatively few training observations and so
reducing variance is crucial. In contrast, QDA is recommended if the training set is very large, so that the variance of
the classifier is not a major concern, or if the assumption of a common covariance matrix for the K classes is clearly
untenable.

4. K-NEAREST NEIGHBORS
▲ Simple and intuitive. It is simple and easy to explain to laypeople.
▲ Non-parametric, therefore, it doesn’t have any assumptions on the data distribution
▲ No training step: KNN is more of an exception to the general machine learning workflow. It doesn’t have a
training/validation/test set. The model created with KNN is available in a labeled dataset, placed in metric
space. Say, if you want to classify any object, the model has to read through all the data and compare the
distances of the closest objects.
▲ Easy to implement for multi-class problems: Compared to other algorithms, it is very easy to predict
multiclass problems. Just supply the ‘k’ a value that is equivalent to the number of classes and you are good to
go.
▲ Few hyperparameters: When working with K-NN, you just need to provide two parameters, k (the numbers
of neighbors to consider) and the choice of Distance Function (e.g. Euclidean, Manhattan distance).
▲ Used for classification and regression: It can be used for classification and regression
▲ Instance-based learning (lazy learning): You don’t need to fit a model in advance, just provide the data point
and it will give you the prediction.
24

4. K-NEAREST NEIGHBORS
▼Slow with a larger dataset. If it is going to classify a new sample, it will have to read the whole dataset,
hence, it becomes very slow as the dataset increases.
▼Curse of dimensionality: KNN is more appropriate to use when you have a small number of inputs. If
the number of variables grows, the KNN algorithm will have a hard time predicting the output of a new
data point.
▼Feature inputs need to be scaled: It is a must that the features should be scaled. KNN uses distance
criteria, like Euclidean or Manhattan distances, therefore, it is very important that all the features have
the same scale.
▼Outlier sensitivity: KNN is very sensitive to outliers. Since it is an instance-based algorithm based on
the distance criteria, if we have some outliers in the data, it is liable to create a biased outcome.
▼Missing Value not treated: It is not capable of treating or dealing with missing values
▼Class imbalance can be an issue: If we have an imbalanced class data, the algorithm might wrongly
pick the majority class.

2. APPROXIMATION-GENERALIZATION TRADEOFF
2.1. BIAS AND VARIANCE
Problems associated with Bias-Variance
High Bias - Low Variance (Underfitting): Predictions are consistent, but
inaccurate on average. This can happen when the model uses very few parameters
and is unable to capture the underlying pattern of the data.
High Bias - High Variance: Predictions are inconsistent and inaccurate on average.
Low Bias - Low Variance: It is an ideal model.
Low Bias - High Variance (Overfitting): Predictions are inconsistent and accurate
on average. This can happen when the model uses a large number of parameters
and when our model captures the noise along with the underlying pattern in data.

Exercise 4: What is the effect of an Expansionary Monetary Policy?
The neutrality of money
•
In the short run, a monetary expansion leads to an increase in output, a decrease
in the interest rate, and an increase in the price level.
•
In the medium run, the increase in nominal money is reflected entirely in a
proportional increase in the price level. The increase in nominal money has no
effect on output or on the interest rate.
•
The neutrality of money in the medium run does not mean that monetary policy
cannot or should not be used to affect output.

text:
Exercise: Unemployment and Labor Force Participation in Spain
Suppose the following data describe Spain’s working-age population in a year:
Employed people: 21 million
•
Unemployed people who are actively seeking work: 2 million
•
People who are not working and are not seeking work: 17 million
•
Answer the following questions:
1. Calculate Spain’s labor force.
2. Calculate the unemployment rate.
3. Calculate the labor force participation rate.
4. Explain why people who are not actively seeking work are not counted as
unemployed.
56

Answer Key
1. Labor force
Labor force = 21 million employed + 2 million unemployed = 23 million people
2. Unemployment rate
Unemployment rate = (2 million ÷ 23 million) × 100 = 8.7%
3. Labor force participation rate
Working-age population = 21 million + 2 million + 17 million = 40 million people
Labor force participation rate = (23 million ÷ 40 million) × 100 = 57.5%
4. Explanation
People who are not working and are not actively looking for a job are classified as outside
the labor force, not as unemployed. To be considered unemployed, a person must be
without work, available to work, and actively seeking employment.

3. Five Different Kinds of Unemployment
3. The Natural Rate of Unemployment
• The natural rate of unemployment is what would prevail if the economy
were not in a recession or expansion.
• These medium-run changes can be divided into two kinds:
•Frictional
•Structural
• The underlying rates of frictional and structural unemployment change only
slowly through time as major, long-lasting features of the economy change.
• The natural rate changes only slowly through time and the actual rate of
unemployment varies around the natural rate.

outline_path: Session 17, 18, 19 › 3. Five Different Kinds of Unemployment
text:
3. Five Different Kinds of Unemployment
4. Frictional Unemployment
•Results when workers are changing jobs in a dynamic economy.
•Short term unemployment caused by the ordinary difficulties of matching
employee to employer.
•Jobs are constantly being created and destroyed.
•The process of seeking a new job could result in temporary unemployment.
•Some amount of frictional unemployment is efficient.
•Instead of accepting the first available job, workers take time to match their
skills with demands of firms.

outline_path: Session 17, 18, 19 › 3. Five Different Kinds of Unemployment
text:
3. Five Different Kinds of Unemployment
4. Frictional Unemployment
• Finding a job that you want at a wage that you will accept, and the employer
will pay takes time.
• This leads to frictional unemployment.
• Scarcity of information is one of the causes of frictional unemployment.
• In the United States, most of the natural rate of unemployment is frictional.
• The labor market operates relative smoothly.
• The same is not necessarily true in Europe.

Persistent, long-term unemployment caused by long-lasting shocks or permanent
•
features of an economy that make it more difficult for some workers to find jobs.
Possible causes:
•
labor market institutions: unemployment benefits, the level of minimum
•
wage, hiring and firing costs
restructuring as a result of globalization,
•
new information technologies, AI
•
the shift from manufacturing to services.

5. Structural Unemployment
It has significant costs:
•
- Loss of economic output.
- The unemployed suffer higher levels of stress, higher rates of suicide, and lower
rates of measured happiness.
• Structural unemployment has been a more serious problem in Europe than in the US
because of labor regulations:
- Unemployment benefits, minimum wages, unions, and employment protection laws
benefit workers.
- All of these regulations are more generous and wide-ranging in Europe.
- These regulations can increase unemployment rates.

4. Wage Determination
• Sometimes wages are set by collective bargaining: a bargaining between trade unions and
firms.
• Slightly more than 10% of U.S. workers’ wages are set by collective bargaining (BLS).
•In Spain, 92.1% of employees eligible for collective bargaining were covered by a
collective agreement in 2024 (OECD).
• Collective bargaining plays an important role in Japan and most European countries.
•The higher the skills needed to do the job, the more likely there is to be bargaining
between employers and individual employees.

4. Wage Determination
• Workers are typically paid a wage exceeding their reservation wage:
the wage that would make them indifferent between working or being
unemployed.
• Wages typically depend on labor-market conditions: The lower the
unemployment rate, the higher the wages.
• Given these two facts, economists have focused on two broad lines of
explanation:

4. Wage Determination
1. Workers’ bargaining power depends on:
◦How costly is for the firm to find other workers: NATURE OF JOB
◦How hard it is for workers to find another job if they were to leave the firm:
LABOR MARKET CONDITION
P. Diamond, D. Mortensen and C. Pissarides received the 2010 Nobel Prize in
Economics for working out the characteristics of a labor market with large flows
and wage bargaining. https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2010/prize-announcement/

4. Wage Determination
2. Efficiency wage theories link the productivity of the efficiency of workers to
the wage they are paid.
• Firms may want to pay a wage above the reservation wage in order to decrease
workers’ turnover and increase productivity.
• Firms that see employee morale and commitment as essential to the quality of
workers’ work will pay more than those whose activities are routine.
• When unemployment is low, firms that want to avoid an increase in quits will
increase wages to induce workers to stay with the firms.

4. Wage Determination
Example: Henry Ford and Efficiency Wages
Table 1 Annual Turnover and Layoff Rates (%) at Ford, 1913–1915
• In 1914, Henry Ford, the builder of Model-T, announced that his company would pay all qualified
employees a minimum of $5.00 a day for an eight-hour day, compared to previously an average
$2.30 for a nine-hour day.
• The turnover rate (ratio of separation to employment) plunged from 370% in 1913 to 16% in
1915: 31% of workers left each month.
• The layoff rate collapsed from 62% to nearly 0%.
• The average rate of absenteeism ran close to 10% in 1913 and decreased to 2.5% in 1914

unemployment.
2. Recessions are periods (lasting at least two quarters) in which real GDP
falls (negative growth).

4. Depreciation, the Trade Balance, and Output
• Real depreciation affects the trade balance through three
separate channels:
1. Exports, X, increase.
2. Imports, IM, decrease.
3. The relative price of foreign goods in terms of
domestic goods, 1/ε , increases.
• Marshall-Lerner condition: A real depreciation leads to
an increase in net exports.
• Depreciation leads to a shift in demand, both foreign and
domestic, toward domestic goods. The shift in demand
leads, in turn, to both an increase in domestic output and
an improvement in their trade balance.

Balance
• An increase in investment must be reflected either
an increase in private saving or public saving, or
in a deterioration of the current account balance.
• A deterioration in the government budget balance
must be reflected in an increase in either private
saving, or in a decrease in investment, or else in a
deterioration of the current account balance (net
exports).
• A country with a high saving rate must have
either a high investment rate or a large current
account surplus.

• Financial wealth, or wealth, is the value of all your
financial assets minus all your financial liabilities, and it
is a stock variable
• Investment is what economists refer to as the purchase
of new capital goods.
• Financial investment is the purchase of shares or other
financial assets.

Open market operations (OMOs) and setting the federal funds rate
are both essential tools used by the U.S. Federal Reserve to influence
monetary policy. The relationship between them is key to how monetary
policy is implemented.
1. Federal Funds Rate as the Target
•The federal funds rate is the primary tool or target the Federal Reserve
uses to influence the broader economy. The Federal Open Market
Committee (FOMC) meets regularly to set a target range for the federal
funds rate, which is the interest rate at which banks lend to each other
overnight.
•The federal funds rate refers to the interest rate at which banks and
other depository institutions lend excess reserves to each other overnight.
2. Open Market Operations as the Tool to Achieve the Target
•While the Fed sets a target for the federal funds rate, it doesn’t directly
dictate that rate. Instead, the Fed uses open market operations to
adjust the supply of reserves in the banking system, thereby guiding the
actual federal funds rate toward the desired target.

Traditional (old) cost accounting
•
Historically, companies produced a limited variety of products.
•
These companies used few overhead resources to support these simple
operations, so indirect (or overhead) costs were a relatively small percentage
of total costs.
•
Managers used simple costing systems to allocate overhead costs broadly in
an easy, inexpensive, and reasonably accurate way.
•
But as product diversity and indirect costs increased, broad averaging led to
inaccurate product costs. That’s because simple peanut-butter costing (that’s
what it’s called) broadly averages or spreads the cost of resources uniformly to
cost objects (such as products or services) when, in fact, the individual
products or services use those resources in nonuniform ways.

Traditional (old) cost accounting
•
Under costing and over costing. Broad averaging often leads to under costing
or over costing of products or services:
•
Product under costing: a product is reported to have a low cost per unit
but consumes a higher level of resources per unit.
•
Product over costing—a product is reported to have a high cost per unit
but consumes a lower level of resources per unit.
•
Under cost products will be underpriced and may even lead to sales that
actually result in losses because the sales may bring in less revenue than the
cost of resources they use.
•
Over cost products will lead to overpricing, causing those products to lose
market share to competitors producing similar products.

Traditional (old) cost accounting
•
The following example illustrates how averaging can result in inaccurate and
misleading cost data (Undercost: James. Overcost: Emma)
•
Product-cost cross-subsidization means that if a company undercosts one of its
products, it will overcost at least one of its other products. Similarly, if a
company overcosts one of its products, it will undercost at least one of its
other products. Product-cost cross-subsidization is very common when a cost
is uniformly spread—meaning it is broadly averaged—across multiple products
without managers recognizing the amount of resources each product
consumes.

Refining the costing system
There are three main guidelines for refining a costing system:
1. Direct-cost tracing. Identify as many direct costs as is economically feasible.
2. Indirect-cost pools. Expand the number of indirect-cost pools until each pool is
more homogeneous. All costs in a homogeneous cost pool have the same or a
similar cause-and-effect (or benefits-received) relationship with a single cost
driver that is used as the cost-allocation base.
3. Cost-allocation bases. Whenever possible, managers should use the cost driver
(the cause of indirect costs) as the cost-allocation base for each homogeneous
indirect-cost pool (the effect).

ABC: Activity Based Costing
One of the best tools for refining a costing system is activity-based costing. Activity-based
costing (ABC) refines a costing system by identifying individual activities as the fundamental
cost objects. An activity is an event, task, or unit of work with a specified purpose—for example,
designing products, setting up machines, operating machines, or distributing products.
To help make strategic decisions, ABC systems identify activities in all functions of the value
chain, calculate costs of individual activities, and assign costs to cost objects such as products
and services on the basis of the mix of activities needed to produce each product or service.
The logic of ABC systems is twofold:
1) First, when managers structure activity cost pools more finely, using cost drivers for each
activity cost pool as the cost-allocation base, it leads to more accurate costing of activities.
2) Allocating these costs to products by measuring the cost allocation bases of different
activities used by different products leads to more accurate product costs.

Cost hierarchies (I)
A cost hierarchy categorizes various activity cost pools on the basis of the different
types of cost drivers, cost-allocation bases, or different degrees of difficulty in
determining cause-and-effect (or benefits-received) relationships.
ABC systems commonly use a cost hierarchy with four levels to identify cost-
allocation bases that are cost drivers of the activity cost pools:
1) Output unit–level costs. The costs of activities performed on each individual
unit of a product or service. Machine operations costs (such as the cost of energy,
machine depreciation, and repair) related to the activity of running the
automated molding machines are output unit–level costs because, over time, the
cost of this activity increases with additional units of output produced (or
machine-hours used).

Cost hierarchies (II)
(2) Batch-level costs. The costs of activities related to a group of units of a product or
service rather than each individual unit of product or service. Example: the cost of the
machine setup activity varies with the setup hours needed to produce batches (groups) of
different products regardless of the total number of products produced.
(3) Product-sustaining costs. The
costs
of
activities
undertaken
to
support
individual
products
or
services
regardless

number
of
units or batches in which the units are
produced or services provided. Example: cost of designing a product.
(4) Facility-sustaining costs. The costs of activities that managers cannot trace to
individual products or services but that support the organization as a whole. Example:
headquarters admin costs.

Takeaways
Broad averaging (or “peanut-butter costing”) describes a costing approach that uses broad averages
for assigning (or spreading, as in spreading peanut butter) the cost of resources uniformly to cost
objects.
Over costing may result in overpricing and competitors entering a market and taking market share for
products that a company erroneously believes are low-margin or even unprofitable. Under costing
may result in companies selling products on which they are in fact losing money, when they
erroneously believe them to be profitable.
Costing system refinement means making changes to a simple costing system that reduces the use of
broad averages for assigning the cost of resources to cost objects and provides better measurement
of the costs of overhead resources used by different cost objects. Three guidelines for refinement
are:
1.Classify as many of the total costs as direct costs as is economically feasible.
2.Expand the number of indirect cost pools until each of these pools is more homogenous.
3. Use the cause-and-effect criterion, when possible, to identify the cost-allocation base for
each indirect-cost pool.

Takeaways
An ABC approach focuses on activities as the fundamental cost objects. The costs of these activities are
built up to compute the costs of products, and services, and so on.
An ABC approach attempts to use cost drivers as the allocation base for indirect costs, whereas a
simple costing system generally does not. The ABC approach classifies as many indirect costs as direct
costs as possible.
Cost allocation starts with the distinction between direct and indirect costs. When both direct and
indirect costs are calculated for a cost object, then the full cost of a cost object is calculated. The full

Management Control Concepts

Management Control concepts
•
Financial accounting focuses on reporting financial information to external
parties such as investors, government agencies, banks, and suppliers based on
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP).
•
Management accounting is the process of measuring, analyzing, and reporting
financial and nonfinancial information that helps managers make decisions to
fulfill the goals of an organization.
•
Cost accounting provides information for both management accounting and
financial accounting professionals. Cost accounting is the process of
measuring, analyzing, and reporting financial and nonfinancial information
related to the costs of acquiring or using resources in an organization.

Management Control concepts
Management control = managerial accounting:
•
“The process of obtaining, creating, and analyzing relevant
information to help achieve organizational goals”.
•
“The process by which managers influence other organizational
members to implement organizational strategies” (Anthony and
Govindarajan, 2007).

Support to design the corporate strategy
A company’s strategy specifies how the organization matches its own capabilities
with the opportunities in the marketplace. In other words, strategy describes how
an organization creates value for its customers while distinguishing itself from its
competitors.
Management accountants work closely with managers to formulate strategies
by providing information about the sources of competitive advantage, such as:
(1) the company’s cost, productivity, or efficiency advantage relative to competitors
(2) the premium prices a company can charge over its costs from distinctive product
or service features

✓Will adequate cash be available to fund the strategy, or will additional funds need to
be raised? (M&A)

Key management accounting guidelines

Cost-Profit approach
Revenues – total variable costs – total fixed costs = Operating profit
Selling Price * Q – (VC per unit * Q) – total FC = Profit
E.g. Company manufactures a microchip
Price = $ 10.15
Direct labor/unit = $ 2
Direct material/unit = $ 1.3
Variable overhead/unit = $ 4.4
Fixed overhead costs for the microchips = $ 450.000
How many microchips do we need to sell to break even?

Cost-Profit approach
SP*Q – (VC*Q) – FC = 0
10.15 Q – 7.7 Q – 450,000 = 0
Q = 450,000 / 2.45 = 183,674 microchips

Assets
An asset is a resource that is expected to provide future
economic benefits (i.e. generate future cash inflows or reduce
future cash outflows).
2 criteria to recognize an asset:
1. It is acquired in a past transaction or exchange, and
2. The value of its future benefits can be measured with a
reasonable degree of precision.

Enron
• Large natural gas pipeline co. Was doing great until 2000: $ 100.8
billions of revenues and $979 millions in earnings.
• Filled bankruptcy in 2001
• They violated several accounting rules
• One of them was to create Special Purpose Entities and transferred
debt to them which did not show on Enron’s accounts

Liabilities
A liability is a claim on assets by “creditors” (non-owners) that
represents an obligation to make future payments of cash, goods or
services. Criteria to consider a liability:
1. The obligation is based on benefits or services received currently
or in the past
2. The amount and timing of payment is reasonably certain.

Revenues
Revenues are recognized when:
1. Are earned (goods or services are provided)
2. It is realized (i.e. payment for goods or services is received in cash or
something that can be converted to a known amount of cash)
Companies can get aggressive in accounting for revenues (50% of the
enforcement actions of the SEC are for violation of one of these two
criteria).

Expenses
Expenses are recognized when:
•
Related revenues are recognized (product costs) or
•
Incurred, if difficult to match with revenues (period costs and unusual
events)
Conservatism principle (unusual events): recognize anticipated losses
immediately (e.g. an environmental cleanup, severance to workers upon
restructuring), anticipated gains only when realized

Market-based transfer prices

Market-based transfer prices
3 conditions for using market-based transfer prices:
• Market of intermediate product is perfectly competitive
• Interdependencies between subunits are minimal
• No additional costs/benefits from selling/buying externally
instead of internally
In general, companies prefer their managers to buy/sell
internally

Market-based transfer prices
A perfectly competitive market exists when there is a homogeneous product with buying prices equal to selling
prices and no individual buyers or sellers can affect those prices by their own actions. By using market-based
transfer prices in perfectly competitive markets, a company can (1) promote goal congruence, (2) motivate
management effort, (3) evaluate the performance of subunits, and (4) preserve their autonomy.
When supply outstrips demand, market prices may drop well below their historical averages. If the drop in prices
is expected to be temporary, these low market prices are called “distress prices.” Deciding whether a current
market price is a distress price is often difficult.
If markets are not perfectly competitive, selling prices affect the quantity of product sold. Faced with an
imperfectly competitive market, the manager of the selling division will choose a price and quantity combination
for the intermediate product that maximizes the division’s operating income. If the transfer price is set at this
price, the buying division may find that acquiring the product is too costly and results in a loss and decide not to
purchase the product.

text:
The Budget as a management tool
A budget is:
✓(a) the quantitative expression of a proposed plan of action by
management for a specified period and
✓(b) an aid to coordinate what needs to be done to implement that plan.
The budget generally includes both the plan’s financial and nonfinancial
aspects and serves as a road map for the company to follow in an upcoming
period.
You project not only P&L but also B/S, cash flow statements, operations and
key performance indicators.

text:
The Budget as a management tool
Responsibility and controllability
Budgetary slack: the practice of underestimating budgeted revenues or
overestimating budgeted costs to make budgeted targets easier to achieve.
Stretching targets: they are challenging but must be achievable to exert
extra effort but avoiding excess of anxiety or demotivation.
Ethics: At no point should the pressure for performance embedded in
stretch targets push employees to engage in illegal or unethical practices.

Budget & Strategy
Budgeting is most useful when it is integrated with a company’s strategy.
Strategy specifies how an organization matches its capabilities with the
opportunities in the marketplace to accomplish its objectives.

Budgets and the budgeting cycle
• The master budget expresses management’s
operating and financial plans for a specified period. It
includes:
• budgeted income statement
• budgeted balance sheet
• the cash budget
• capital expenditures budget
• the budgeted statement of cash flows.
• Additional complexity in multinationals: exchange
rates, different tax rates, inflation…

Master budget
The master budget expresses management’s operating and financial plans
for a specified period, usually a fiscal year, and it includes a set of
budgeted financial statements. The master budget is the initial plan of
what the company intends to accomplish in the period and evolves from
both the operating and financing decisions managers make as they
prepare the budget:
✓Operating decisions deal with how to best use the limited resources of
an organization.
✓Financing decisions deal with how to obtain the funds to acquire those
resources.

Budgeting cycle
1. Managers at all levels take into account the company’s past
performance, market feedback, and anticipated future changes to
initiate plans for the next period.
2. At the beginning of the fiscal year, senior managers give subordinate
managers a frame of reference, a set of specific financial or
nonfinancial expectations against which they will compare actual
results.
3. During the course of the year, management accountants help
managers investigate any deviations from the plansand if necessary,
corrective action.

Steps in preparing a Budget
✓Start by Identifying the problem and uncertainties: strategy and
challenges
✓Obtain accurate info: from the company and the market…
✓Make predictions about the future: i.e. assumptions to project,
macro trends, competition…
✓Make decisions by choosing among alternatives: i.e. new products
o markets, capex versus return, investment plan…
✓Implement the decision, evaluate performance and learn

Sensitivity analysis
✓Analyze how budgets may perform under different assumptions
used in the projections (i.e. change in the product mix sales, costs
of materials, competition, inflation…)
✓Base, pessimistic and optimistic cases
✓Worse case scenario
✓Contingency plans and remedial actions

The Cash budget
The cash budget is a schedule of expected cash receipts and cash
disbursements. It predicts the effects on the cash position at the given
level of operations. Main sections:
✓Cash available for needs before financing
✓Cash disbursements: inventory purchases, manufacturing costs,
labor, outlays for properties, capex, taxes…
✓Short and long term financing needs and investment opportunities
✓Ending cash balance
✓Goal: determine feasibility of the operating plan

Static budgets vs. Flexible budgets
Static budget: budgeted revenues and costs based
on the level of output planned (at the start of the
budget period)
Flexible budget: budgeted revenues and costs
based on the actual output (at the end of the budget
period)

Variances
Variance = difference between actual results and
budgeted (standard) results
Variances are used to:
-
Find out and correct the problem
-
Evaluate performance and motivate managers
-
Potential change in the strategy

Variance Analysis
• Used to control performance
• Allows to determine the different sources of
variance
• Allows management by exception

text:
Users, Groups and File Ownership
●
The file system stores data and metadata, while the OS checks which processes
may access them.
●
A user account has a numeric user ID (UID). Processes run with user identities,
which the OS uses to check access.
●
A group has a group ID (GID) and can include several users. Each user can
belong to several groups.
●
Each file and directory has one owner UID and one group GID. These are
metadata associated with its inode.
●
In our container, id reports UID 1001 and GID 1001 for analyst. The numbers
match here, but identify different things.
●
User and group names make these IDs easier to read. Permissions decide what
those identities are allowed to do.
2

outline_path: Session 10 › Nine Bits, Three Permission Classes
text:
Nine Bits, Three Permission Classes
●
Looking at the .bashrc file, -rw-r--r-- starts with - for a regular file, followed
by three triplets: rw-, r--, r--.
●
The triplets apply to the owner, group and others, in that order. Others means
users who match neither owner nor group.
●
For a regular file, r allows reading, w allows changing its contents, and x allows
execution. A dash means that permission is absent.
●
The OS first checks the process’s user identity. If it matches the file owner, only the
owner triplet applies.
●
Otherwise, a matching group uses the group triplet. If neither matches, the others
triplet applies. The triplets are not added together.
●
Here, analyst can read and edit .bashrc, while group members and others can
read it, provided they can reach its directory.
4

Permissions on Directories
●
On a directory, r lets a process list entry names, while x lets it look up those
names and traverse the directory.
●
Directory w, together with x, normally permits creating, renaming and removing
entries. File w controls the contents instead.
●
A file can therefore be deleted without write permission on that file, if its parent
directory permits removal.
●
The initial d means directory. Our home (.) is drwxr-x---, so the `others` class
of users cannot reach files inside.
●
The + on work signals extra access-control information, e.g., an access-control list
(ACL). The nine bits may not describe all access rules.
5

Inspect Permissions Before Changing Them

text:
FAT: How a File Is Found
●
Storage is divided into pieces of equal size, called clusters. The data of a file
occupy one or more clusters.
●
The clusters of a file do not have to be next to each other. FAT can use any free
cluster, wherever it is, so a file can grow without needing one long empty region.
●
The FAT has one entry for each cluster. The entry says which cluster comes next
in the same file, or that this cluster is the last one (-1 in the figure).
●
The directory entry of a file records two things: the number of its first cluster and
the size of the file.
●
To read a file, the OS goes to the first cluster, looks up its entry in the table to find
the second, and repeats until it reaches the last. This sequence is the FAT chain.
●
In the figure, File A starts at cluster 4. The table then leads to clusters 7, 2, 10 and
12, where the file ends.
10

FAT: Costs and Limitations
●
Following a chain means reading many table entries. Reading them from disk
would be slow, so the OS keeps a copy of the table in RAM, called a cache.
●
The cache only speeds up finding where the data are. The data themselves must
still be read from storage.
●
The table has one entry per cluster, so a larger disk means a larger table and more
RAM for the cache.
●
Example: A 1 TB disk with 4 KB clusters has about 250 million clusters. At 4 bytes
per entry, the table takes about 1 GB, half the RAM of our container.
●
When RAM is short, the OS keeps in RAM only the parts of the table in use and
reads the rest from disk when needed.
●
The last cluster of a file is rarely full, so some space in it stays unused.
●
The clusters of a file can be far apart, which slows reading on a hard disk as
seeking the start of the following cluster costs time (especially a mechanical one).
11

Alternatives to FAT
●
Other file systems avoid the chain used by FAT.
●
Some keep, for each file, a list of all its blocks. Others record multiple extents for
each file: "start at this block and continue for this many blocks".
●
Example: ext4 is a common Linux file system that stores the starting point of a
file's extent list in its inode.
●
Journaling protects the file system's own records:
a.
It writes a note of what it is about to do before changing a record.
b.
It can finish or undo a half-made change after a crash.
●
Note: Journaling is not a backup. Data written just before a crash can still be lost.

When Does the Scheduler Run?
●
The OS must choose a process to run when:
○
a new process is created: should the parent or the child run?

A non-preemptive scheduler lets a process run until it blocks, exits or gives up the

A preemptive scheduler can stop a process at a timer interrupt and run another

Linux, macOS and Windows are preemptive. Many early batch systems were not.

text:
How Long Should a Time Slice Be?
●
Each switch costs time: the OS saves and restores registers and runs the scheduler, and the
next process starts with cold caches.
●
With 4ms slices and 1ms per switch, 1ms in 5 is lost: 20% of the CPU. With 100ms slices,
about 1%.
●
Long slices hurt response time: with 50 ready processes and 100ms slices, the last one can
wait 5s.
●
This is amortization: pay a fixed cost less often, as when we batch system calls (Lecture 5).
●
Tanenbaum suggests 20–50ms as a compromise. Linux aims for slices of a few milliseconds.

outline_path: Session 12 › Linux Took a Different Route
text:
Linux Took a Different Route
●
In 2003, Linux 2.6 introduced the O(1) scheduler, a close relative of MLFQ, with 140 priority levels
and a queue for each level.
●
Linux calls what it schedules a task: a process, or one thread of a process. OSTEP, and our
animations, call them jobs.
●
It always ran the first task in the highest-priority non-empty queue. Finding that task took the same
time however many tasks were waiting: hence the name O(1).
●
Each task sat in one of two sets of queues, active or expired. A task that used up its time slice moved
to expired; when active was empty, the two sets swapped.
●
Like MLFQ, O(1) guessed from past behavior which tasks were interactive: tasks that often slept got
a priority bonus, those that used a lot of CPU got a penalty.
●
The guesses were complex and often wrong.
Since 2007, Linux no longer guesses: each task gets a fair share of the CPU, set by a nice value.

Single-queue scheduling: every core takes its next process from one shared queue.

It is simple, and it balances the load: no core is idle while processes wait.

outline_path: Session 13 › Why We Build HPC Clusters
text:
Why We Build HPC Clusters
●
Some problems are too big for one computer: their data does
not fit in one node's memory, or their work would take months on
one node.
●
Weather forecasts, climate models, drug design, genomics,
financial risk and the training of AI models all run on clusters of
many nodes.
●
Meta trained its Llama 3 language model (405 billion
parameters) with 3.8 x 1025 operations, on 16,000 GPUs in 2,000
servers. One 4-CPU job on our cluster would need about 5
million years.
●

Standard Stream Redirection
●

>> : redirect stdout appending its content to the target
○

2> : redirect stderr
○

The Operating System as a Resource Manager
●
OS provides for an orderly and controlled allocation of the processors, memories, and I/O
devices among the various programs wanting them.
●
OS keeps track of which programs are using which resource, to grant resource requests, to
account for usage, and to mediate conflicting requests from different programs and users.
●
Example:
a.
Three programs running on a computer try to print simultaneously on the same printer. What
happens?
b.
Chaos: The first few lines of printout might be from program 1, the next few from program 2, then
some from program 3, and so forth.
c.
The OS buffers all the output, and when one program is finished the OS sends its output from the
disk file where it has been stored to the printer.
●
Resource management includes multiplexing (sharing) resources in two different
ways: in time and in space.
a.
Time: different programs or users take turns using the resource (e.g., computing cycles of a CPU)
b.
Space: different programs or users get a part of the available resource (e.g., memory/disk space)

Time Sharing
●
A CPU (or any physical processing unit) can run only one process at a time.
●
With only a few physical CPU cores available, how can the OS provide the illusion
of a nearly endless supply of cores, i.e., one for each active process?
●
OS use time sharing: running one process, then stopping it and running another,
and so forth.
●
Slicing the available processing time across multiple sequential processes and
doing it very fast (1000 times/s), gives the illusion of parallel process execution.
●
Question: Do we have a performance penalty compared to running the same
processes, each on a dedicated physical core?
●
Question: Recall the related notion of space sharing? Do we use it in our laptops
and computers?
9

Mechanisms and Policies
●
Implementing time sharing requires both capabilities and rules to make decisions
about when to share the available resources across multiple processes.
●
Mechanisms are low-level methods or protocols that implement a needed piece of
functionality, e.g., stop a process and start another one.
●
Policies are algorithms for making some kind of decision within the OS. For
example, given a number of possible programs to run on a core, which program
should the OS run?
●
Scheduling policies make decisions about processes, e.g., based on:
a.
Historical information, e.g., which program has run more over the last minute?
b.
Workload knowledge, e.g., what types of programs are run
c.
Performance metrics, e.g., is the system optimizing for interactive performance,
or throughput?

Concurrency and Parallelism In Multicore Architectures
●
Concurrency: the ability to manage multiple processes whose total execution
periods overlap in time, e.g., time-sharing executes P1, then P2, then P1, etc.
●
Parallelism: running multiple processes at the exact same time on separate
hardware cores or processors
●
We have heterogeneous processing units (CPU, GPU, TPU, ...) with multiple cores
●
OS use time-sharing to achieve concurrency on a single core, and parallelism to
do so on multiple cores at the same time.
●
This increases the pool of processes that can be active at the same time, but can
slow down each executing process due to the performance of each core
●
Note: OS using multiple cores != process using multiple cores.
●
We will explore in depth the latter in the second part of the course looking at
parallel computing and parallel programming

Anatomy of a Process
●
A process is an activity of some kind with a program, input, output, and a state
●
When executing, a process has:
○
Memory: program’s instructions lie in memory, and the data that the running program reads and
writes sits in also memory.
○
Registers: many instructions explicitly read or update CPU registers
○
Persistent storage: I/O information might include a list of the files the process currently has open.
●
The OS exposes a process application programming interface (API):
○
Create: When we type a command into the shell, or double-click on an application icon, the OS is
invoked to create a new process to run that program.
○
Destroy: Usually, processes run and exit by themselves when complete; when they don’t, the
user/OS need a way to kill them
○
Wait: wait for a process to stop running, e.g., before collecting output and analyzing it.
○
Control: E.g., suspend a process (stop it from running for a while) and then resume it (continue it
running).
○
Status: get some status information about a process as well, such as how long it has run for, or

Process Initialization
●
How does a process start? An existing process executes a system call to create
the new process, telling the OS which program to run in it.
●
In *nix, the system call to create a new process is fork:
○
Creates a clone of the calling process, same memory image, environment strings, open files.
○
The child process then executes a similar call to change its memory image and run a new program.
●
In Windows, the Win32 system call is CreateProcess:
○
Handles both process creation and loading the correct program into the new process
○
Has 10 parameters, including the name of the program to execute.
○
Win32 has about 100 other functions for managing and synchronizing processes and related topics!
●
The parent and child process have distinct memory spaces. If either process
makes a change, the change is not visible to the other process.
●
Note: in common OSs, the first process to launch when we start our computer is
hard-coded into the OS booting image.
15

Process Termination and Hierarchy
●
How does a process stop? usually due to one of the following conditions:
○
Normal exit (voluntary): the process has done its work and executes a system call to tell the OS
that it is finished, and its allocated resources can be relinquished.
○
Error exit (voluntary): the process discovers a fatal error, announces the fact, and issues the exit
system call as with a normal exit.
○
Fatal error (involuntary): the process caused and error, returning an error code or raising a CPU
exception, both intercepted by the OS that kills (gracefully) the process.
○
Killed by another process (involuntary): another process with suitable privileges issues a
terminating system call for the process.
●
Hierarchy of processes:
○
In most OSs, when a process creates another process, the parent process and child process
continue to be associated in certain ways
○
UNIX initialization: the init process forks off a new process per terminal. If a login is successful,
the login process executes a shell to accept commands and each command forks other processes.
○
All the processes in the whole system belong to a single tree, with init at the root.
○
Windows has no concept of a process hierarchy. All processes are equal.
16

Process States
●
A process can be in different states:
○
Running: executing instructions on a processor.
○
Ready: ready to run but the OS has chosen not to run it
at this given moment.
○
Blocked: not ready to run until some other event takes
place. E.g., when a process initiates an I/O request to a
disk, it becomes blocked and thus some other process
can use the processor.
●
The OS:
○
Moves a process between the ready and running states,
i.e., (de)scheduling.
○
Keeps a process blocked (e.g., when it initiates an I/O
operation) until some event occurs (e.g., I/O completion)
○
Moves an unblocked process to the ready state again
and then to running again, depending on policies.
