outline_path: Session 5 › No Such a Thing As a Free Lunch
text:
No Such a Thing As a Free Lunch
●
Threads share memory. That gives them speed and power… And danger.
●
Race condition:
a.
Definition: two threads read the same value, each modifies it, and the result depends on which thread
happened to modify the value first.
b.
Classic example: two workers each add 1 to a shared counter. Worker A and B reads 10, A adds 1,
saves 11, B adds 1, saves 11. The counter ends up at 11, not 12.
c.
Silent killer: The answer is wrong, but no exception is risen. The program silently makes mistakes
that are difficult and time consuming to debug, usually also for a LLM.
d.
Non-deterministic: the same code on the same data can give a different answer on different runs,
e.
Timing-dependent: notoriously, they disappear when you add a print statement to investigate them,
e.g., B arrives after A writes due to time taken to print and the counter is 12.
●
Processes don't have this problem by default: they don't share memory, so they
can't race on it.
●
Processes have the mirror-image problem: to cooperate, they must copy data to
each other which costs time and requires safe coordination with 3+ processes.
6

outline_path: Session 5 › No Such a Thing As a Free Lunch
text:
No Such a Thing As a Free Lunch
●
Mutual exclusion rule: code that access shared data is called a “critical region”
and we must have at most one thread inside the critical region at a time.
●
Solutions to enforcing this rule:
a.
Sleep awaken: whoever leaves the region awakens the next thread.
b.
Mutex ("mutual exclusion lock"): lock before entering the critical region, unlock after.
c.
Semaphore: a counter for when we must have "at most N at a time" rather than "exactly one".
d.
Built-in: build the locking into the language, so we cannot forget to unlock, e.g., Python with lock.
e.
Message passing: not sharing memory at all, send copies instead as with processes. This is what
multiprocessing queues and MPI do, and it's the model of Part II.
f.
Barrier: wait until every thread reached a condition, then all threads start again.
●
Every one of these costs time. E.g., a lock serializes execution because the
protected part runs one-at-a-time no matter how many cores we have.
●
Priority inversion: a low-priority thread with a lock can stall a high-priority one.
●
Avoiding locks altogether, e.g., techniques like read-copy-update (RCU),
Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC), Software Transactional Memory (STM)
7

outline_path: Session 5 › Why User and Kernel Modes?
text:
Why User and Kernel Modes?
●
Goal: share one machine safely without trusting every application.
●
Protecting the system from potential failures or malicious activities by managing how
applications interact with system resources like files, memory, I/O, and network.
●
User Mode:
a.
Isolation: Applications run in user mode within their own virtual memory space. This means one
application cannot access or modify the memory of another application.
b.
Crash Protection: If an application crashes, it does not affect the operating system or other
applications, maintaining overall system stability.
c.
Limited Access: User mode restricts access to critical operating system resources, preventing
applications from inadvertently damaging essential system data.
●
Kernel Mode:
a.
Shared Memory Space: All code running in kernel mode shares a single virtual address space. This
means that if a kernel-mode driver fails, it can lead to a system-wide crash.
b.
Critical Operations: Kernel mode handles essential tasks such as memory management (Lecture
6–7), process scheduling (lecture 10), and hardware communication.
8

outline_path: Session 5 › Why Do We Need a Boundary?
text:
Why Do We Need a Boundary?
●
Imagine every program could write to the disk directly, with no permission check.
a.
Any program could overwrite any file, including other users’ files and the OS itself.
b.
A buggy loop could scribble over the memory of your browser, your bank session, everything.
c.
Nothing could be shared safely: no multi-user machines, no cluster, no cloud.
●
Mechanisms to enable separation of user/kernel modes:
a.
Applications make requests: they name a service, supply arguments, and receive a value or error.
b.
The OS kernel configures the rules: it defines valid entry points, process memory mappings,
identities, and permissions.
c.
Hardware enforces the boundary: the CPU and memory-management hardware check what the
current code is allowed to do:
■
The processor records an architectural privilege level
■
Checks on memory permissions and privileged-instruction prevent unauthorized access.
●
In this way, software (OS) and hardware (processing units) work together to maintain
separation of concerns and thus the security and stability of the whole system.
●
Software defines policy while hardware ensures that applications cannot simply bypass it.
9

outline_path: Session 5 › Kernel Events and the System-call Trap
text:
Kernel Events and the System-call Trap
●
Three types of events can enter the OS kernel:
a.
System call: an intentional request made by a running process. E.g., a process calling
read(fd, …) asks the kernel to obtain data from a file.
b.
Exception or fault: an event detected by the CPU while executing the current instruction.
E.g., a page fault, divide-by-zero operation, or invalid instruction.
c.
Interrupt: an event from outside the current instruction stream. E.g., a timer tick,
completed disk operation, or arriving network packet.
●
System call:
a.
Setup: placing the system-call number and arguments in the CPU registers.
b.
Execute a special instruction: requests to entry in protected kernel mode (called trap).
c.
Hardware changes execution state: the CPU changes privilege and executes the
requested operation
10

Syscalls And Python
●
Python often provides both low-level and high-level interfaces:
○
For files, os.open(), os.read(), os.write(), and os.close() closely resemble
Unix system calls. The built-in open() and file objects provide a safer and more
convenient abstraction.
●
We use low-level interfaces when precise control matters:
○
Low-level calls are useful in operating-system tools, servers, runtimes, databases, and
embedded software.
●
We normally use abstractions for application development as higher-level APIs
reduce code and prevent common mistakes. E.g.:
○
With open(...) over manually calling os.open() and os.close()
○
subprocess.run() over manually combining fork(), exec(), and wait()
○
Requests or httpx over manually using sockets
○
Device-specific libraries over issuing raw ioctl() operations
14

Syscalls And Python
●
File system calls reveal that files are OS-managed resources.
○
Open a file descriptor (fd) from the OS; read/write transfer bytes; close releases fd.
○
Python file objects hide this lifecycle, but underneath they rely on the same OS services.
●
Process system calls explain how programs are created and controlled.
○
On Unix, fork creates a child process, exec replaces a process with another program,
wait collects a child’s result, and kill sends a signal.
○
Python exposes these through os, although subprocess and multiprocessing are usually
more portable and easier to use.
●
Memory calls explain how Python obtains memory from the OS.
○
Operating systems provide mechanisms such as brk and mmap to modify a process’s
address space.
○
Python’s interpreter and memory allocator normally manage this automatically.
○
We use mmap.mmap() directly for memory-mapped files, shared memory, or efficient
access to large data; Python does not provide a standard direct brk() wrapper.
15

Syscalls And Python
●
Network abstractions are ultimately built on sockets:
○
socket, connect, send, and related calls establish endpoints and transfer bytes.
○
Libraries for HTTP, APIs, databases, and distributed systems sit on top of sockets and
add protocols, encryption, authentication, timeouts, retries, and data serialization.
●
Device calls provide a path to hardware-specific operations:
○
ioctl performs operations that do not fit normal byte-oriented read and write behavior.
○
In Python, it is exposed through fcntl.ioctl() on Unix.
○
Used for terminals, cameras, network interfaces, sensors, or custom drivers, but
specialized libraries are usually safer and easier.
●
We study system calls even when frameworks usually hide them:
○
They explain what high-level operations actually cost and why programs block, fail, leak
resources, or behave differently across operating systems.
○
Understanding them helps us diagnose performance problems, choose suitable
abstractions, reason about concurrency and security, and recognize when a framework
16
cannot provide the control we need.

outline_path: Session 6 › Pages: Memory in Fixed-Size Blocks
text:
Pages: Memory in Fixed-Size Blocks
●
The OS hands out an address space to each process made of pages, typically each
page is 4 KB.
●
The OS maintains exclusive access to the physical RAM and organizes the physical
RAM in a list of frames of the same size as the pages.
●
The OS keeps a page table for each process to track which virtual page maps to
which physical frame.
●
Note: A page does not have to be in RAM!
a.
It may be unused by the process, e.g., input data that still need processing
b.
Parked on disk, e.g., when unused by the process or when the OS is context switching processes.
●
The CPU consults this mapping on every memory access, billions of times/s.
8

outline_path: Session 6 › Swap: Extending RAM On Disk
text:
Swap: Extending RAM On Disk
●
Swap extends system memory by using NVMe SSD/HDD as a spillover zone.
●
Memory management technique where the OS temporarily moves active/inactive
data from physical RAM onto storage (known as swap space).
a.
Active data: we run out of RAM and instead of killing the processes, we use the much slower storage
b.
Inactive: Relocating inactive background memory pages from physical RAM to storage drives frees up
premium RAM for active tasks at the cost of slower storage speeds.
c.
Virtualized memory: using the swap to run processes that require more memory than the RAM
●
We want as much RAM as possible in our system:
a.
The more RAM we have the less the OS has to use the swap (if at all)
b.
The OS can cache input data directly in RAM while moving stagnant pages to the swap.
c.
The OS can create a so-called zram space into the RAM to serve the process swapping logic instead
of using a much slower swap. Note that zram trades CPU cycles for memory space.
●
Note: relying too heavily on swapping on disk wears out hardware, forcing non-stop
read/write cycles that degrade the lifespan of a solid-state drive.
9

outline_path: Session 6 › Why Is Translation Not Super Slow?
text:
Why Is Translation Not Super Slow?
●
The CPU keeps a small, very fast cache of recent translations called the TLB
(Translation Lookaside Buffer).
●
Programs touch the same few memory pages over and over, so the TLB hit rate is
typically well above 99%.
●
This is the same principle as caching everywhere else:
a.
Exploit locality: the TLB cache is local and physically near to the core/CPU
b.
Optimize the common case: processes hits over and over the same page.
●
When code jumps around memory randomly, the TLB cannot help. This is one
reason scattered accesses are much slower than sequential ones. More in Part II.

outline_path: Session 6 › What If The OS Loses The VIRT Gamble?
text:
What If The OS Loses The VIRT Gamble?
●
If the process starts writing data to every page it was promised, the transition from
VIRT to RES forces the OS into a resource crunch.
●
Performance Drop (thrashing phase):
a.
As the process fills up the physical RAM, the OS scrambles to free up space using our storage drive.
b.
The OS spends its time moving pages back and forth, between RAM and disk.
c.
Result: Our system enters a state called thrashing. The mouse cursor freezes, UI elements stop
responding, and the entire computer slows to a near-total crawl.
●
Out-Of-Memory (OOM) Killer strikes:
a.
If the swap space fills up too, the next time our process tries to write to a new memory address, the
CPU triggers a Page Fault but the OS has zero physical frames left to hand out.
b.
To save itself from a total system crash, the OS activates the OOM killer.
c.
The OS calculates a "badness score" for every running application and our process that is actively
chewing through massive amounts of memory will be immediately terminated.

text:
Page Fault: Asking For a Memory Page
●
Page fault: type of hardware interrupt or exception raised by the Memory
Management Unit (MMU) when a program tries to access a memory page that is
not available or cannot be accessed.
●
What causes a page fault:
a.
Demand Paging: The operating system loads pages into RAM only when requested, meaning initial
access to a new page naturally triggers a fault.
b.
Swapped Out Data: The required data was previously moved from RAM to secondary storage (disk
or swap space) to free up space.
c.
Invalid Access: The program requests a memory address it has no permission to access or that does
not exist, causing a fatal error.
●
Page faults can be soft, hard, or invalid:
a.
Soft: The requested data is already in RAM but is not marked in the specific process’ page table or
resides in a standby list; the OS just updates the mapping.
b.
Hard: The requested data is not in RAM and must be fetched from secondary storage (e.g., disk I/O),
which takes significantly longer.
3
c.
Invalid: The memory address is illegal or unauthorized, resulting in a segmentation fault.

Page Eviction and Replacement
●
Under memory pressure, the OS evict pages from RAM and reuse their frames,
while keeping the pages in their process’s virtual address spaces.
●
E.g., the OS discards
a.
Unused file-backed pages and reload them from their file when needed.
b.
Unused pages from swap (if available).
●
The OS evict a page that will not be needed soon. Accessing an evicted page
causes a page fault and requires reloading its contents, i.e., it costs time!
●
LRU (Least Recently Used) policy: pages not accessed recently are less likely to be
accessed soon.

Swapping
●
The OS moves cold, infrequently accessed pages to swap and reuse their physical
frames. This can happen in the background, before a process needs more memory.
●
Storage I/O is expensive: servicing a fault can take ms with a mechanical disk. The
actual delay depends on the storage device, its load, and the I/O required.
●
Occasional swapping can work well: moves rarely used pages out of RAM with little
impact if the evicted pages are not needed again soon.
●

text:
Out of Memory (OOM) Killer in Linux
●
Activation: Triggered when fail to free up memory.
●
Goal: Sacrifices offending process to rescue system stability.
●
The process that triggers the OOM is not necessarily the
process that gets killed
●
Computes a per-process "badness" score based on how much
memory or swap a process uses of its allocation.
●
Userspace can bias that score to make a process ineligible.
●
The OOM victim is not necessarily the process that triggered the fatal allocation, not
the single biggest memory user.
●
Our demo scripts (07_oom_demo.py, 07_oom_multi_demo.py,
07_oom_stall_demo.py) show the basic kill, choice three competing processes
of different sizes and protection levels, and a OOM failures with system freeze.

outline_path: Session 7 › Linux vs. Windows/macOS: Two Different Bets
text:
Linux vs. Windows/macOS: Two Different Bets
●
Windows and macOS generally avoid Linux-style aggressive
overcommit
●
Windows imposes a memory request limit, and an exceeding
request fails not allowing the process to start so no innocent
bystander gets killed later.
●
macOS leans on memory compression and swap first, but does
have a OOM analogue called jetsam
●
Jetsam picks processes by priority type (background/idle apps first,
foreground apps last) rather than a single computed score
●
Neither OS exposes an "opt out of being killed" option as Linux.

outline_path: Session 7 › Linux vs. Windows/macOS: Different Tradeoffs
text:
Linux vs. Windows/macOS: Different Tradeoffs
●
Linux's overcommit-and-kill-later model maximizes memory sharing across many
processes, at the cost of unpredictability unless someone actively tunes priorities.
●
Windows/macOS's conservative accounting gives predictable, local failures and a
better single-user experience, at the cost of leaving some memory capacity unused.
●
Context decides the winner:
a.
Linux's approach fits multi-tenant servers and container platforms
b.
Windows/macOS model fits interactive desktops where an allocation simply
returning an error is better than a random background app dying.
●
Neither is "better", each optimizes for what it’s typical workload needs most:
memory utilization versus predictability.

5: Request size and Python buffering
●
Using os.read(), we vary the request from 1 byte to 1 MiB while reading the
same 6 MB file, so the data stay constant.
●
One-byte requests need 6,013,655 Python calls and 1,730.384 ms, while 64 KiB
requests need 93 calls and 0.245 ms.
●
Fewer iterations repeat less Python and kernel work, which explains the large gain
without isolating the cost of a syscall.
●
Further gains can shrink or reverse because the same file must still be copied, and
larger chunks need more temporary memory.
●
Using open() for one-byte reads is 14.6 times faster here because its buffer
serves many requests without entering the kernel.
●
Request size sets how many bytes we receive, while Python's buffer has a
separate capacity of 128 KiB in this container.

outline_path: Session 8 › 5: Many files or one combined file
text:
5: Many files or one combined file
●
We load the same 100,000 records from 1,000 small CSV files and from one
combined file, then check that both return equivalent data.
●
One combined file avoids repeating file opening and CSV-reader setup, which can
otherwise dominate many small loads.
●
In this run, the combined file loads in 0.06 s rather than 0.368 s, making each load
about 6.1 times faster.
●
Combining the files first costs 0.749 s, so the 0.308 s saved per later load must
repay that preparation.
●
Three later loads recover the preparation cost, while a single load would not justify
combining the files in this run.
●
Consolidation therefore helps when we revisit the data often enough, e.g., while
adjusting an analysis or rerunning a report.
6

5: Saving results in batches
●
We save the same 5,000 rows using three strategies, so differences in time come
from how we organise the writing.
●
Reopening for every row takes 0.566 s because each row repeats opening, CSV
conversion, writing and closing.
●
Keeping the file open reduces the time to 0.423 s, while 5,000 calls to to_csv()
still repeat slicing and CSV formatting.
●
Keeping it open and writing 500 rows per batch needs only ten to_csv() calls
and takes about 0.004 s.
●
All three outputs contain identical bytes, showing that batching reduces repeated
work while preserving the saved result.
●
Batches give the largest saving here, while larger batches can need more memory
and delay when new results are saved.
7

6A: Measuring the loaded table
●
Loading the CSV turns 100,000 rows and nine columns into Pandas arrays and
other objects, so file size does not tell us their memory cost.
●
memory_usage() estimates storage for the columns and row index, giving us a
measure of the table rather than the whole process.
●
For object columns, a shallow estimate can miss the Python objects holding the
values, while deep=True includes those objects.
●
Our text columns use Arrow, a library that stores column data in buffers whose
bytes are already counted in the shallow estimate.
●
Both estimates therefore report 10.56 MiB, and ArrowStringArray confirms the
text representation used in this run.
●
The full analysis needs more memory because Python, libraries, other tables and
temporary calculations also occupy RAM.

6A: Categories can save or cost memory
●
A category stores each distinct label once and gives every row an integer code, so
repeated labels can use less memory.
●
The region column has only six labels across 100,000 rows, and its storage falls
from 1.301 to 0.096 MiB.
●
The customer_id column has 60,417 distinct labels, so it must keep a much
larger label set as well as 100,000 row codes.
●
Its labels and codes use about 1.188 MiB, but a lookup structure adds 2.016 MiB
to help Pandas find each label.
●
The complete category therefore uses 3.204 MiB rather than 1.335 MiB as text,
making it larger despite repeated customer IDs.
●
A category helps only when saved label storage outweighs its codes and lookup
structures, so measure and verify before converting.

●
We check ranges and missing entries before choosing smaller integer types
because those types have limits on the values they can store.
●
order_id values from 1 to 100,000 fit int32, while quantity values from 1 to
20 fit int16.

Repeated labels, including product_id, become categories, while date text
becomes date values to reduce storage.
●

because its category would cost more memory.
●
The same nine-column table now uses 4.27 MiB instead of 10.56 MiB, leaving
more room for joins, calculations or plots.

6B: The table and the Python process
●
VIRT describes the process's virtual address space, while RSS reports the
memory currently resident in RAM.
●
Loading the CSV raises VIRT from 913.0 to 1,943.1 MiB, but that increase does
not mean the process uses that much more RAM.
●
RSS rises from 157.0 to 187.3 MiB, adding about 30.3 MiB even though the loaded
table is estimated at 10.56 MiB.
●
Python may keep memory for reuse after parsing, and RSS also includes the
runtime, imported libraries and other objects.
●
Because the reader creates temporary objects, readings taken only before and
after loading can miss its highest memory use.
●
These readings describe the process, so use the container's memory limit and
other running work when planning the full analysis.

6B: Requesting, using and releasing memory
●
The NumPy experiment separates requesting memory from writing to it: loading a
CSV combines both operations.
●
np.zeros() creates a zero-valued array needing 190.7 MiB of element storage.
In this run, VIRT grows by that amount.
●
RSS stays at 187.7 MiB after allocation: the new address range does not yet need
that much additional RAM.
●
Writing across the array's pages raises RSS to 378.4 MiB. VIRT stays unchanged
because the address range already exists.
●
del big removes the reference and RSS falls to 187.8 MiB, but it may not always
fall: Python and its libraries can keep released memory for later objects.
●
Note: Successful allocation does not prove a later calculation will fit because writes
and temporary objects can increase memory demand.

7: Establishing the regional answer
●
Our question is how much revenue each region generated in 2025. All 100,000
sample transactions belong to that year.
●
For each transaction, revenue = quantity * unit_price. Summing by
region gives the six totals needed for the report.
●
The sample fits in memory, so we first use the complete table to establish a
reference answer.
●
Each alternative must preserve the region labels and agree within half a cent:
using less memory is useful only if the answer holds.
●
We then change what is retained, i.e., fewer columns, smaller representations,
chunks or individual rows.
●
This connects loading and preparation to reporting: the required result determines
which data must remain in memory.

7: Selecting the required columns
●
The report needs region, quantity and unit_price. The other six input
columns do not contribute to this answer.
●
usecols tells pd.read_csv() to retain those three inputs. Note that the full CSV
still has to be scanned, so this does not remove all reading work.
●
After calculating revenue, we keep only region and revenue for each
transaction, while quantity and price have served their purpose.
●
This final two-column table uses 2.06 MiB, compared with 10.56 MiB for the
original nine-column table.
●
All 100,000 rows still contribute and the regional totals agree: we saved storage by
removing fields, without dropping transactions.
●
The 2.06 MiB describes the retained table. Parsing buffers and temporary
calculations also need memory while it is built.

●
With CHUNK_ROWS = 10_000, the sample arrives in ten chunks. In this way, we do
not load all ten into a list.

between chunks, so earlier contributions are preserved.

Removing their references allows storage to be reused.

totals agree with the full-table reference.

With six fixed regions, more rows mean more iterations. Millions of customer
groups would make the retained dictionary grow.

7: Supplying one row at a time
●
revenues_by_region() supplies a region and its revenue for each
transaction, without first building a full table or list.
●
yield supplies one pair and pauses the function. The consuming loop requests
the next pair when it is ready.
●
The consumer adds each contribution to a persistent dictionary. In this way, only
the current row and running totals are needed for the sum.
●
Streaming limits retained input but it does not eliminate memory use. Reader
buffers and generator state still occupy memory.
●
The six totals pass the half-cent check. The largest difference is 0.00000006,
reflecting small floating-point differences.
●
Python converts and processes every row separately. This can take longer than
Pandas operations over a whole chunk.

From RAM to Storage
●
Applications need to store and retrieve information.
●
RAM alone does not meet every storage requirement:
a.
A dataset may be larger than the available RAM.
b.
Process memory is normally released when a process ends, and RAM loses
its contents when power is removed.
c.
Processes have separate address spaces, private to each process.
●
Long-term storage therefore needs to provide:
a.
Capacity for large amounts of information.
b.
Persistence beyond the lifetime of a process or a power cycle.
c.
Controlled access to shared information by multiple processes.
●
Examples of storage media:
a.
Hard disk drives (HDDs) store data on magnetic platters.
b.
Solid-state drives (SSDs) have no moving parts and lower access latency.
c.
Magnetic tape is also used for backups and archives.

text:
Challenges and a New Abstraction
●
Shared storage raises three questions:
a.
How do we find information?
b.
How do we control who can access it?
c.
How do we track which parts of the storage are free?
●
The file abstraction gives programs a logical unit for storing information.
●
A process executes instructions, an address space holds its memory, and a file
can retain its inputs and outputs.
●
Processes create files and read or update existing ones through OS interfaces.
●
Files on persistent storage can survive a process ending or a system restart.
Buffered writes must reach storage to survive power loss.
●
The file system organizes files, names and metadata, and works with the OS to
manage storage and enforce access rules.
3

Studying the File System
●
From a user’s perspective, we will study:
a.
File names, types and encodings explain how programs identify and interpret stored bytes.
b.
Inodes, directories, paths and links explain how the OS locates files and their metadata.
c.
Users, groups, UID/GID and permission bits explain access rights. We interpret ls -l and
introduce sudo.
●
File operations connect storage to processes. We examine sequential and random
access, and how an executable becomes part of a process.
●
From an implementer’s perspective, we will study:
a.
Partitions and UEFI explain where file systems reside and how the system begins loading an OS.
b.
FAT, indexes and extents explain how the file system locates the blocks that hold a file’s data.
c.
Block size, caching, compression and deduplication affect performance and the space needed to
store data.
d.
Free-space tracking, quotas, journaling, consistency checks and backups support storage
management and recovery.
4

File Naming
●
File-name rules depend on the OS and file system.
●
Limits apply to each name and to the whole path.
●
E.g., On a Linux filesystem (e.g., ext4), a name can
contain up to 255 bytes.
●
Case handling also varies:
a.
Unix file systems are commonly case sensitive, so Data.csv and
data.csv can name different files.
b.
Windows is usually case insensitive, but case-sensitive directories
are possible.
●
An extension is a naming convention, e.g., .csv or .py.
a.
Applications and desktop tools may use extensions to choose how
to open files.
b.
Some applications inspect the file content or other metadata to
choose how to open the files, independent on their extensions.
c.
Changing an extension does not convert the contents. A CSV
renamed .xlsx is still CSV data.
5

File Access
●
Sequential access reads bytes in order from the current position:
○
A program may stop before the end. To reread a regular file, it can return to an
earlier position.
○
This access pattern suits media like magnetic tape.
●
Random access lets a program seek to a byte offset before reading
or writing:
○
Regular files normally support both sequential and random access.
○
Seeking changes the offset for an open file. It does not itself read data or physically
move a disk head.
●
Example: an indexed reservation file can locate one record without
scanning all earlier records.
●
The storage device affects performance and trade offs:
○
An HDD may need to move its head, so scattered access can be slow.
○
An SSD has no moving head, but access size and locality still matter.

Checks access and returns a file descriptor for later I/O. It does not read the whole file.

Common file operations and Linux interfaces
Operation
Description
Append
Writes at the end of the file. Linux uses write() on a file opened with O_APPEND, rather
than a separate append syscall.
Seek
Changes the offset used by later reads or writes on a seekable file. It does not itself
transfer data. Linux provides lseek().
Get attributes
Retrieves metadata such as size, ownership and permissions, e.g., through stat().
Set attributes
Changes permitted metadata fields, e.g., chmod() changes permission bits. The process
must have authority to make the change.
Rename
Changes a name or location within the same file system without copying the file’s
contents. Across file systems, mv normally copies the data and then removes the source.

COURSE DESCRIPTION
5
This course offers an introduction to Organizational Behavior, a field on human
•
differences, emotions, perceptions, behaviors, and interactions within the context of
work organizations.
More specifically, the topics include personality, attitude, emotion, and motivation at
•
the individual level, as well as leadership, communication, diversity, and conflict at the
group/organizational level.
This course addresses issues such as understanding individual differences, motivating
•
employees with various needs, leading groups and teams, resolving conflicts in an
organizational context and, eventually, building a high-growth and sustainable
organization where people will flourish.
* From the Syllabus

LEARNING OBJECTIVES AND SKILLS
6
In this course, students will:
•
1.
Raise awareness and sensitivity regarding the impact of human-related issues in
the workplace.
2.
List basic organizational behavior principles and explain how these principles
influence human behavior in the workplace.
3.
Analyze individual human behavior by using knowledge of personality, attitudes,
emotions, and motivations.
4.
Understand group behavior elements, such as leadership, power, politics,
communication, conflict, and negotiation.
5.
Enhance critical thinking skills through case studies, class discussions, and group
projects.

METHODOLOGY & PREREQUISITES I
7
The course is based on IE University teaching method is defined by its
•
collaborative, active, and applied nature.
Students actively participate in the whole process to build their knowledge
•
and sharpen their skills.
Professor’s main role is to lead and guide students to achieve the learning
•
objectives of the course.

METHODOLOGY & PREREQUISITES II
8
This is done by engaging in a diverse range of teaching techniques and different types
•
of learning activities such as: cases, articles, videos, self-evaluation tools and a
significant amount of in-class discussion and dialogue.
To fully take advantage of each session along this OB course, it is important that you

are prepared to engage in a rich exchange of ideas during the sessions.
Thus, prior to each class, read the assigned materials carefully and critically and prepare

your answers following the outlines in the syllabus.

investigates the impact that individuals, groups, and
structure have on behavior within organizations for the
purpose of applying such knowledge toward improving an
organization’s effectiveness.

Organizational behavior is an applied behavioral science

that is built upon contributions from a number of
behavioral disciplines:
– Psychology
– Social Psychology
– Sociology
– Anthropology

Personality Determinants
– Early argument → Is personality the result of heredity or

The Dark Triad:
– Machiavellianism: the degree to which an individual is
pragmatic, maintains emotional distance, and believes that ends
can justify means.
– Narcissism: the tendency to be arrogant, have a grandiose sense
of self-importance, require excessive admiration, and have a
sense of entitlement.
– Psychopathy: the tendency for a lack of concern for others and a
lack of guilt or remorse when their actions cause harm.

18
Strengths and Weakness of the MBTI and Big Five
Model (6 of 6)
An emerging framework to study dark side traits:
•
– First, antisocial people are indifferent and callous toward others.
– Second, borderline people have low self-esteem and high
uncertainty.
– Third, schizotypal individuals are eccentric and disorganized.
– Fourth, obsessive compulsive people are perfectionists and can
be stubborn, yet they attend to details, carry a strong work ethic,
and may be motivated by achievement.
– Fifth, avoidant individuals feel inadequate and hate criticism.

outline_path: Session 5 › FROM EMOTIONS TO EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE
text:
FROM EMOTIONS TO EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE
6
EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE:
•
A person’s ability to perceive emotions in the self and others, understand the
–
meaning of those emotions, and regulate their own emotions accordingly.
The case FOR it: intuitive appeal, it predicts criteria that matter such as job
–
performance, and it has a biological basis.
The case AGAINST it: the concept is defined too broadly, it is difficult to measure,
–
and its validity is disputed. Know both sides — you will be asked about "EQ" in an
interview before you are asked about anything else from this course.
EMOTIONAL LABOR:
•
Expressing organizationally desired emotions during interpersonal transactions.
–
Surface acting is linked to emotional exhaustion and burnout; deep acting is not.
–
EMOTION REGULATION
•
Is the trainable part: surface acting, deep acting, emotional suppression, cognitive
–
reappraisal, social sharing, mindfulness.
Suppression is expensive and often ineffective. Reappraisal works.
–

Your team presentation must cover Attitudes and Emotions. This is

Criticisms of Herzberg’s theory:

18
Compare the Early Theories of Motivation (6 of 7)
• McClelland’s Theory of Needs
– The theory focuses on three needs:
• Need for achievement (nAch): drive to excel, to achieve in
relation to a set of standards, to strive to succeed.
• Need for power (nPow): need to make others behave in a
way that they would not have behaved otherwise.
• Need for affiliation (nAfl): desire for friendly and close
interpersonal relationships.

outline_path: Session 5 › Compare the Early Theories of Motivation (7 of 7)
text:
19
Compare the Early Theories of Motivation (7 of 7)
McClelland’s theory has had the best research
•
support cross-culturally
– It has less practical effect than the others.
– Because McClelland argued that the three needs are
subconscious—we may rank high on them but not know
it—measuring them is not easy.
– It is more common to find situations in which managers
aware of these motivational drivers, label employees based
on observations made over time.

outline_path: Session 5 › Self-Determination Theory vs. Goal-Setting Theory (1 of 9)
text:
20
Self-Determination Theory vs. Goal-Setting Theory (1 of 9)
• Self-Determination Theory
– People prefer to feel they have control over their
actions.
• Focus on the beneficial effects of intrinsic motivation and harmful
effects of extrinsic motivation.
• Cognitive evaluation theory - When people are paid for work, it feels
less like something they want to do and more like something they
have to do.
• Proposes that in addition to being driven by a need for autonomy,
people seek ways to achieve competence (mastery) and positive
connections to others.

outline_path: Session 5 › Self-Determination Theory vs. Goal-Setting Theory (2 of 9)
text:
21
Self-Determination Theory vs. Goal-Setting Theory (2 of 9)
Self-Determination Theory
•
– When extrinsic rewards are used as payoffs for
performance, employees feel they are doing a good job.
• Eliminating extrinsic rewards can also shift an individual’s perception
of why they work on a task from an external to an internal
explanation.
– Self-determination theory acknowledges that extrinsic
rewards can improve even intrinsic motivation under
specific circumstances:
• Deadlines and specific work standards do, if people believe they are
in control of their behavior
• Rewards and deadlines diminish motivation if people see them as
coercive.

outline_path: Session 5 › Self-Determination Theory vs. Goal-Setting Theory (3 of 9)
text:
22
Self-Determination Theory vs. Goal-Setting Theory (3 of 9)
Self-Determination Theory
•
– What does self-determination theory suggest for
providing rewards?
– Self-concordance:
• Recent outgrowth of SDT
• Considers how strongly people’s reasons for pursuing goals
are consistent with their interests and core values.
– If individuals pursue goals because of an intrinsic interest, they are
more likely to attain their goals and are happy even if they do not.
– The process of striving toward them is fun (hedonism)

outline_path: Session 5 › Self-Determination Theory vs. Goal-Setting Theory (4 of 9)

Self-Determination Theory vs. Goal-Setting Theory (4 of 9)
Self-Determination Theory / Self-concordance
•
– What does all of this mean?
• For individuals:
– Choose your job for reasons other than extrinsic rewards.
» Employees who feel what they do is within their control and a result
of free choice are likely to be more motivated by their work and
committed to their employers.
• For organizations:
– Provide intrinsic as well as extrinsic incentives. They need to:
» make the work interesting,
» provide recognition,
» link organizational and employee goals, and support employee
growth and development.

•
– Intentions to work toward a goal are a major source of

needed.
Evidence suggests:
•
1. Specific goals increase performance.
2. Difficult goals, when accepted, result in higher performance
than do easy goals.
3. Feedback leads to higher performance than does non-feedback.

Self-Determination Theory vs. Goal-Setting Theory (9 of 9)
• Goal Setting and Ethics
• The relationship between goal setting and ethics is
quite complex:
– If we emphasize the attainment of goals, what is the cost?
– Time pressure often increases as we are nearing a goal, which
can tempt us to act unethically to achieve it.
• We may forgo mastering tasks and adopt avoidance
techniques so we don’t look bad, both of which can
incline us toward unethical choices.

Self-efficacy theory is an individual’s belief that they

Enactive mastery: gaining relevant experience with the task or job

Reinforcement theory: behavior is a function of its

– Reinforcement conditions behavior.
– Behavior is environmentally caused.
Goal setting is a cognitive approach: an individual’s
•
purposes direct their actions.
Operant conditioning theory: people learn to behave to get

something they want or to avoid something they don’t
want.
– B.F. Skinner’s behaviorism.

Distinguish Between Different Types of Groups (1 of 5)
• A group is defined as two or more individuals, interacting
and interdependent, who have come together to achieve
particular objectives.
• Groups can be either formal or informal:
• Formal groups: those defined by the organization’s
structure
– e.g. an airline flight crew
- Informal groups: alliances that are neither formally
structured nor organizationally determined
-
e.g. natural formations in the work environment in response to the
need for social contact, three employees from different
departments who regularly eat lunch together is an informal
group.

text:
12
Distinguish Between Different Types of Groups (2 of 5)
• Why do people form groups?
– Our tendency to take personal pride or offense for the
accomplishments of a group is the territory of social identity
theory.
• Social Identity Theory: considers when and why individuals
consider themselves members of groups.
– People have emotional reactions to the failure or success of
their group because their self-esteem gets tied into the
performance of the group.
– Social identities help us understand who we are and where we
fit in with people.

Distinguish Between Different Types of Groups (4 of 5)
• Ingroups and Outgroups
– Ingroup favoritism:
• Probably the biggest downside in social identities
• occurs when we see members of our group as better than other

outgroup
• is sometimes everyone else,

outline_path: Session 10, 11 › Distinguish Between Different Types of Groups (5 of 5)
text:
15
Distinguish Between Different Types of Groups (5 of 5)
• Social Identity Threat
– Ingroups and outgroups pave the way for social
identity threat, which is akin to stereotype threat.
– Individuals believe they will be personally negatively
evaluated due to their association with a devalued
group, and they may lose confidence and performance
effectiveness.

THE PUNCTUATED-EQUILIBRIUM MODEL (9.2)
16
Temporary groups working to a deadline do not pass through the
•
usual stages of development. They follow their own sequence:
The first meeting sets the group's direction.
–
The first phase is one of inertia: the group does comparatively little.
–
A transition takes place exactly when the group has used up half of its
–
allotted time.
The transition triggers major changes: old patterns are dropped and new
–
ones adopted.
A second phase of inertia follows the transition.
–
The group's last meeting is marked by markedly accelerated activity.
–
Translation for your presentation: you will do very little until around
•
the second week of November, and then everything at once. That is
not a character flaw, it is the model — and knowing it is what lets you
move your own midpoint forward.

17
ROLES AND THE PSYCHOLOGICAL CONTRACT (9.3, 1 of 2)
Role: a set of expected behavior patterns attributed to someone
•
occupying a given position in a social unit.
Role perception: your own view of how you are supposed to act in a given
–
situation, learned from the stimuli around you (colleagues, friends, books,
films.)
Role expectations: how OTHERS believe you should act in that same
–
situation.
The psychological contract: the unwritten agreement between
•
employee and employer that sets out mutual expectations — what
management expects of you, and what you expect of management.
It appears in no contract, and it governs most of what people feel about
–
their job.
When it is broken, satisfaction, commitment and performance all fall
–
immediately.

ROLE CONFLICT (9.3, 2 of 2)
18
Role conflict: when an individual faces divergent role expectations, so
•
that complying with one makes complying with another more
difficult.
Interrole conflict: when the expectations of your different groups are in
–
opposition. E.g.: the student who is also an employee and also a son or
daughter meets this weekly.
Most employees belong simultaneously to an occupation, a work group, a
–
division and several demographic groups, and those roles do not always
agree with each other.
The managerial move is not to remove the conflict: It is to make the
•
expectations explicit.
Most role conflict is produced by assumptions nobody has ever said out
–
loud.

NORMS AND CONFORMITY (9.4, 1 of 3)
19
Norms: acceptable standards of behavior within a group, shared by
•
the group's members. They tell members what they ought and ought
not to do in given circumstances.
Norms cover performance, appearance, informal social arrangements and
–
the allocation of resources. Almost none of them are written down
anywhere.
Norms and emotions: norms can dictate what people are allowed to feel in
–
a group, and how they are permitted to show it.
Conformity: adjusting your behavior to align with the norms of the
•
group. The groups you want to belong to (your reference groups)
exert the strongest pull of all.
Asch's experiments: asked to match the length of lines, around a third of
–
participants gave an answer they could plainly see was wrong, because
everyone before them had said it.

DEVIANT WORKPLACE BEHAVIOR (9.4, 2 of 3)
20
A group with strong positive norms lifts behavior across an organization, which is
–
what corporate social responsibility initiatives try to create.
A group with strong negative norms does the same in reverse, and deviance is
–
contagious.
Deviant workplace behavior: voluntary behavior that violates significant
•
organizational norms and, in doing so, threatens the well-being of the
organization or its members.
PRODUCTION: leaving early, working slowly on purpose, wasting resources.
–
PROPERTY: sabotage, lying about hours worked, stealing from the organization.
–
POLITICAL: showing favoritism, gossiping and spreading rumors, blaming
–
coworkers.
PERSONAL AGGRESSION: harassment, verbal abuse, stealing from coworkers.
–
People who are socially isolated are more likely to engage in it. People in
•
groups where it is normal are far more likely still. The group predicts it
better than the person does.

NORMS AND CULTURE (9.4, 3 of 3)
21
Do people in collectivist cultures have different norms from people in
•
individualist cultures?
Yes. Collectivists are more likely to conform to group norms, and they
–
experience stronger pressure to do so.
The effect is not only national. Anyone socialized into a strong team culture
–
conforms more inside it, wherever they are from.
For a manager working across countries: silence in a meeting means
•
different things in different places. Do not read agreement into it.

24
of 3)
• Group size affects the group’s overall behavior.
Large groups are good for gaining diverse input.
–
Smaller groups are better doing something with input.

• Social loafing:
the tendency for individuals to expend less effort when working
–

COHESION AND GROUP EFFECTIVENESS (9.6)
25
Cohesion: the degree to which group members are attracted to one another and
•
motivated to stay in the group.
Cohesion affects productivity, but the direction depends entirely on the group's
–
performance norms:
High cohesion + high performance norms → HIGH productivity
•
High cohesion + low performance norms → LOW productivity
•
Low cohesion + high performance norms → MODERATE productivity
•
Low cohesion + low performance norms → LOW to moderate productivity
•
The dangerous cell is high cohesion with low performance norms: a group that
•
likes each other and has silently agreed not to work hard. It is also the most
pleasant cell to sit in, which is why it survives so long.
To increase cohesion: make the group smaller, build agreement on goals,
–
increase time spent together, raise the group's status, stimulate competition with
other groups, reward the group rather than the individual.

Group Decision Making Intro – Question for the class
• Are group decisions better than those made by
individuals alone?
– Strengths of group decision making
– Weaknesses of group decision making

27
Group Decision Making (1 of 8)
• Strengths of group decision making:
– More complete information and knowledge
– Increased diversity of views
– Increased acceptance of solutions
• Weaknesses of group decision making:
– Time consuming
– Conformity pressures
– Dominance of a few members
– Ambiguous responsibility

28
Group Decision Making (2 of 8)
• Effectiveness and efficiency of group decisions:
– Accuracy
– Speed
– Creativity
– Acceptance

29
Group Decision Making (3 of 8)
• Groupthink:
– Is related to norms and affects decision making
– Describes situations in which group pressures for conformity
deter the group from critically appraising unusual, minority, or
unpopular views.
• Groupshift:
– Also known as group polarization
– a change between a group’s decision and an individual
decision that a member within the group would make.
– Groups generally shift toward a more extreme version of the
group’s original position.

30
Group Decision Making (4 of 8)
• Most group decision making takes place in interacting
groups
– Members meet face-to-face and rely on both verbal and
nonverbal interaction to communicate with each other.
• Interacting groups often censor themselves and pressure
individual members toward conformity of opinion.

31
Group Decision Making (5 of 8)
• Brainstorming can overcome pressures for conformity.
– In a brainstorming session:
• The group leader states the problem.
• Members then “free-wheel” as many alternatives as they
can.
• No criticism is allowed.
• One idea stimulates others, and group members are
encouraged to “think the unusual.”

32
Group Decision Making (6 of 8)
• The nominal group technique:
– Restricts discussion or interpersonal communication
during the decision making process.
• Group members are all physically present, but members operate
independently.
• Permits the group to meet formally but does not restrict
independent thinking, as does the interacting group.
– Nominal groups outperform brainstorming groups.

33
Group Decision Making (7 of 8)
• Steps for a nominal group:
1.
Each member independently writes down their ideas
on the problem.
2.
After this silent period, each member presents one
idea to the group.
3.
The ideas are discussed for clarity.
4. Each group member rank-orders the ideas.
5.
The idea with the highest aggregate ranking
determines the final decision.

outline_path: Session 10, 11 › THE FIVE TYPES OF TEAM ARRANGEMENTS (10.2)
text:
THE FIVE TYPES OF TEAM ARRANGEMENTS (10.2)
40
PROBLEM-SOLVING TEAMS: five to twelve employees from the same department,
•
meeting a few hours a week to discuss improving quality, efficiency and the work
environment. They recommend; they rarely have authority to implement.
SELF-MANAGED WORK TEAMS: typically ten to fifteen people who take on their
•
former supervisor's responsibilities, planning and scheduling work, assigning tasks,
controlling the pace, making operating decisions. The evidence on their effectiveness
is mixed.
CROSS-FUNCTIONAL TEAMS: employees at a similar hierarchical level but from
•
different work areas, brought together to accomplish a task. Effective on complex
problems, and slow in the early stages while trust is built.
VIRTUAL TEAMS: teams that use technology to tie together physically dispersed
•
members. They need deliberate effort on trust, on monitoring progress, and on
making the team's work visible to the organization.
MULTITEAM SYSTEMS: a collection of two or more interdependent teams that share at
•
least one common goal. A team of teams, and leadership of the whole system, not of
each team, is what decides whether it works. It is the arrangement most large
organizations are actually running.

TEAM STATES (10.3)
47
Team states are the shared attitudes and feelings that develop as a
•
team works together. They shape performance as much as the
processes do.
MOTIVATION: the team's collective drive to accomplish the task.
–
TEAM EFFICACY: the shared belief that the team can succeed. Success
–
produces it, and it then produces more success.
TEAM IDENTITY: how far members feel the team is part of who they are.
–
Strong identity means better performance and more satisfied members.
TEAM COHESION: members emotionally drawn to one another and
–
committed to staying.
TEAM TRUST: willingness to be vulnerable to the actions of the other
–
members. The hardest to build and the quickest to lose.

HOW ORGANIZATIONS CREATE TEAM PLAYERS (10.4)
SELECTING: hire for the interpersonal skills that teamwork requires,
•
not only the technical ones. Some organizations use cluster hiring -
recruiting a group of people together rather than one at a time.
TRAINING: teamwork skills can be developed. Workshops on
•
problem solving, communication, negotiation, conflict management
and coaching produce measurable improvement.
REWARDING: if the reward system recognizes only individual
•
contribution, you will get individual behavior whatever you say about
teamwork.
The honest summary: organizations ask for teamwork and pay for
•
individual performance, and then wonder why they do not get
teams.

outline_path: Session 10, 11 › WHEN TO USE INDIVIDUALS INSTEAD OF TEAMS (10.5)
text:
49
WHEN TO USE INDIVIDUALS INSTEAD OF TEAMS (10.5)
Teams are not free. They cost more time and more coordination than
•
individual work, and they are not always better.
Three questions before you form one:
•
1.
Can the work be done better by one person? If the task can be completed
without input from others, an individual is the right choice.
2. Does the work create a common purpose or set of goals for the group
that is more than the sum of individual goals?
3. Are the members genuinely interdependent? Does the success of each
depend on the success of the whole?
If any answer points away from a team, you are about to pay the full
•
cost of a team without receiving its benefit.

IMPLICATIONS FOR MANAGERS - TEAMS
50
Start with the work to be accomplished, not with the team. Decide
•
first whether the work needs a team at all.
Create the context: adequate resources, effective leadership, a
•
climate of trust, and a reward system that reflects team
contributions.
Keep team size small. Large teams are where social loafing lives.
•
Diversity may hurt performance at first and help it later. Expect the
•
growing pains instead of concluding that the team does not work.
Team leaders should establish a common plan and purpose, and
•
build team efficacy and a shared mental model.
Select, train and reward for teamwork. All three, or none of them
•
work.

Cold war: Customers are the same, but firms serve two different types of tastes (segment

Stand up battle: Firms have similar business models and compete for the same space in

of customers (i.e. B2B vs. B2C).

•
TOP DOG: This strategy implies that the post-entry behavior of a company is aggressive, and there is a high
level of entry barriers in the market. The incumbent retaliates when it sees the entrance of a new player.
•
FAT CAT: This strategy implies that the post-entry behavior of a company is accommodating, and there is a high
level of entry barriers in the market. The incumbent does not retaliate when it sees the entrance of a new
player, as they know the entering competitor will also be accommodating.
•
LEAN & HUNGRY: This strategy implies that the post-entry behavior of a company is aggressive, and there is a
low level of entry barriers in the market. The incumbent retaliates when it sees the entrance of a new player.
This implies competition will increase in the market.
•
PUPPY DOG: This strategy implies that the post-entry behavior of a company is accommodating, and there is a

player 2's strategy is the best response to player 1's strategy and player 1's
strategy is a best response to player 2's strategy.

wants to unilaterally deviate to another strategy, given
other players’ strategies
▪A Nash Equilibrium is a set of best-response strategies.

1. Repeated Games
▪What happens if you can “repeat” the same decision? What happens if the
Prisoners can make another decision also after observing the outcome of the
game? The Nash Equilibrium (NE) still stays the same?
▪REPEATED GAMES: Iterated Games are simultaneous games repeated infinite
(finite) times.
Iterations (repetitions) of the game change the NE
1.
Players consider their long-term payoffs instead of short-term gains. This
might lead them to behave differently.
2.
Repetition creates Sub-games (and subgame perfect Nash equilibrium (SPNE))
3.
Repetition creates Learning, Expectations, Trust & Trust Threats
4.
Repetitive interactions might create stability of collusive agreement
(COOPERATION) and Commitment.

2. Dynamic vs. Static Models
▪Dynamic models try to focus on COOPERATION and how price cooperation is
sustainable over time.
• Tit-for-Tat (Spanish →“Dónde las dan las toman”)
Cooperation is a Good strategy on the long run.
Ex.: Oligopolies in general: Electric Oligopoly; Telecom; Financial institutions,…
Failure to cooperate damage the industry on the long run. Ex.: Airlines
• Trigger-grim Strategies
Threatens other players with a “worse," punishment, action if they deviate.
Ex.: The prisoners dilemma, if player A betrays the other, probably player B won´t
ever believe player A.

text:
S13. Game Theory: Applied competition
2. Dynamic vs. Static Models
Tit-for-Tat Strategy (Spanish →“Dónde las dan las toman”)
▪The mere possibility that you play tit-for-tat is sufficient for competitor to
cooperate if the time horizon is long enough.
▪Most managers don’t know how long they will be competing with their rivals,
serving to make COOPERATION IS A GOOD STRATEGY, except near the
end (called end game problem). Thus in a repeated game, prisoner’s dilemma
can have a COOPERATIVE outcome.
▪Industries where only a FEW FIRMS COMPETE under stable demand
cost conditions may COOPERATE even though no contractual arrangements
are made. E. g. Electric companies.
▪FAILURE TO COOPERATE is the result of rapidly shifting demand or cost
conditions, e. g. airlines.
10

action profile.

S14. Lobster Game
1. Instructions of the Lobster Game
Instruction in brief (3/3) → Total rounds 9
Only decide on Quantity (Price depends on Quantity of all the three firms)
1. Rounds 1, 2 & 3 → Cournot NE under Asymmetry of Information
Each boat makes its decision without knowing anything about the others groups’ decisions.
2. Rounds 4, 5 & 6 → Cournot NE under Fist Mover Advantage (FMA)
Alpha (for each island) announces their quantity and the other companies (Bravo & Charlie for the other islands)
decide simultaneously and secretly. Then the other firms do the same on rounds 5 & 6.
3. Rounds 7, 8 & 9 → Cournot NE under Signaling
Alpha (for each island) announce the quantity. This is a signaling not FMA and therefore the company can signal but
it might deviate. Then the other firms do the same on rounds 8 & 9.
4. Round 10 → Collusion agreement
All the firms talks and collude to reach an agreement on quantities.

Observations (2/2)
▪“Out of Equilibrium” scenarios: Firms have an incentive to
unilaterally deviate
• Firms adjust their quantities and move from the ‘out of
equilibrium’ scenario
• The adjustment process continues over an iterated game until
the Equilibrium quantity is reached
▪The Cournot equilibrium industry output does not maximize
industry profits (i.e. it is not pareto optimal; max. for monopoly
quantity and price)
▪By maximizing their own profit independently, in Cournot, firms
produce more output than if they colluded to maximize profits
▪In the Cournot equilibrium, the market price (and profits) reduces if
one of the firms expands its production (unilaterally deviates)

Revenue Destruction Effect
▪Deviations provoke the so called Revenue Destruction Effect
▪Small firms have higher incentive to deviate and disrupt price
stability, because they have a smaller revenue destruction
▪With the number of firms increasing (n higher), the Cournot
prices fall (p lower)
▪Cournot model is often used to plan market reaction in
presence of merges and acquisition by the Antitrust
authorities

▪Signaling theory is useful for describing behavior when two parties
(individuals or organizations) have access to different information.
−Typically, one party, the sender, must choose whether and how
to communicate (or signal) that information, and the other
party, the receiver, must choose how to interpret the signal.
−Signaling theory holds a prominent position in a variety of
management literatures, including strategic management,
entrepreneurship, and human resource management.
▪George Akerlof, Michael Spence, and Joseph Stiglitz received the 2001
Nobel Prize in Economics for their work in information economics.

The three Bain entry conditions
Accommodating Entry

When potential rivals wants to enter there are three different possibilities:
1. Blockaded entry
Existing structural barriers are effective in deterring entry.
2. Accommodated entry
Structural barriers may be low and strategic barriers are ineffective deterring entry
or they are not cost effective.
3. Deterred entry
Entry deterring strategies are effective in discouraging potential rivals and are cost
effective.

3. PREDATORY PRICING → Against CURRENT competitors
•
Incumbent sets a low price to drive smaller rivals from the market (by making it unprofitable for
rivals to stay)
•
The purpose is two: (1) Drive out current rivals. & (2) Deter future rivals from entering

5. Asymmetry of Information and Signaling Theory
Asymmetry of Information and Signaling Theory
Signaling theory is useful for describing behavior when two
parties (individuals or organizations) have access to different
information.
• Typically, one party, the sender, must choose whether and how to
communicate (or signal) that information, and the other party,
the receiver, must choose how to interpret the signal.
• Signaling theory holds a prominent position in a variety of
management literatures, including strategic management,
entrepreneurship, and human resource management.
George Akerlof, Michael Spence, and Joseph Stiglitz received the 2001 Nobel Prize in
Economics for their work in information economics.

2. Stages of Industry Life Cycle
Dominant design vs. Technical Standard
DOMINANT DESIGN → Product architecture that defines the look, functionality,
and production method for the product and becomes accepted by the industry as a
whole. (e.g.: touchpad smartphones; excel type format; message apps)
▪Dominant design ≠ (not always) technical standard
▪A dominant design may or may not embody a technical standard
TECHNICAL STANDARD →Technology or specification that is important for
compatibility (e.g. Android vs. iOS Apple; PDF format; MS Office vs. open Office;
WhatsApp or Telegram)
•
Technical standards typically embody intellectual property in the form of patents or copyrights,
a dominant design usually does not.
•
Technical standards especially emerge when there are network effects (consumers benefit
from using the same standard) (e.g. Andoid vs IOS / Whatsapp vs. Telegram)

S2. Value Creation
From value creation to competitive advantage
▪B-C>0: product is economically viable
▪However, B-C>0 does not imply profit >0
−If several firms create the same economic value, they
compete for consumers by bidding down prices
−Perfect competition firms make zero profit and consumers
capture all economic value
▪For profit>0 in a competitive industry:
(B-C) of Firm 1 > (B-C) of Firm 2
▪Competitive advantage: Lead in B-C compared to other firms
▪Sustainable competitive advantage: Competitors cannot easily
replicate the same B-C

Difficult to estimate cash flows more than 2 or 3 years ahead

Value maximization may encourage short-termism

On existing assets— seek to maximize rate of return

ROI = ROS (Return on Sales) x Capital Turnover
ROI
• ROS = (EBIT / SALES) =
ROS (Return on Sales) → Measures how many profits the company is able to generate given its sales. It is a good
proxy of efficiency of operations, because you can note that you have a sales component both in the numerator and in
the denominator, but in the numerator you have also the cost of good sold component. This is why it could be read as a
good measure of value capture.
EBIT = [ Income – (Cost of Goods sold + other operating cost)
Sales = Turnover (or Business numbers)
• Capital Turnover = (Sales / (Fix assets + Working Capital)
Capital Turnover → Represents how many sales a company it is able to generate given the capital invested. This
measure tends to vary greatly with industry characteristics because industries that require more capital tend to have a
higher denominator. It is a good proxy of value creation, meaning how many sales and volume you are able to
generate given your capital. But no cost proxy is inside this measure.
Sales = Turnover (or Business numbers)
Fix Assets = Long-term tangible piece of property or equipment.
Working Capital = Current Assets – Current Liabilities. Positive working capital indicates that a company can fund its
current operations.

Industry attractiveness on its own is insufficient to justify diversifying into

1. The attractiveness test → Attractive industry?
• The industries chosen for diversification must be structurally attractive or
capable of being made attractive
2. The cost-of-entry test → Increase overall profits?
• The cost of entry must not capitalize all the future profits
3. The better-off test → Create some competitive advantage or synergies?
• Either the new unit must gain competitive advantage from its link with the
corporation or vice versa (i.e. some form of “synergy” must be present)

2. Strategies to reduce Risk of Innovation
3. Big-bet resource investments (shaping)
• Large investment in a tech or business to change current market structure or
prevailing norms and assumptions
• Such a move persuades and signals commitment to partners, suppliers, customers
• Small-scale pivots still possible, but large investments are often irreversible due to
the infrastructure that needs to be developed before innovations can even take place
• Using or creating uncertainty for one’s own advantage
• Famous examples:
• Apple iPhone+Ecosystem (iTunes, Appstore)
• Tesla EVs+charging network + battery Gigafactories
• Microsoft Azure for enterprise software from on-premise licensing to clou-based
infrastructure + subscription model

S25. Strategy in Turbulent Environments
3.4. Chicken and egg problem
4. Chicken-and-egg problem
• Each side waits for the other—solve with price structure (not just price level).
• Subsidize the value-creating side (zero or negative price is sometimes
optimal).
• Potential patterns: free consumers + paid complementors (ad-supported
media); free SDKs/dev tools + paid users (enterprise).
• Non-price seeding: first-party, exclusive, or hit complements
Examples: free players vs. paid servers (Real/Adobe); console bundles; app
store fee holidays.

S25. Strategy in Turbulent Environments
3.5. Complementors
5. Complementors: power, multihoming,
governance
• Complementors are co-strategists; power rises with must-have status and
user access.
• Complementor multihoming weakens tipping; exclusivity can counteract—at a
cost to variety.
• Governance levers: access rules, APIs, quality control; heavy-handedness
invites backlash and regulation.
• Case: Apple v. Epic illustrates holdup risk and the control–goodwill trade-off.

text:
Business Model Innovation
S25.2. Entry Barriers & BMI
Where is the opportunity?
To create an innovative business model should be given a strategic opportunity in the
environment or the industry (Christensen, Johnson and Kagermann, 2008):
1. There is an opportunity to capitalize on new technology. E.g.: + Ipod + Itunes Iphone
(Apple).
2. Within the sector there is a need that is not properly covered. Eg. Fedex, Walmart.
3. When they are changing the basis of competitive rules. You can change what is considered
acceptable in the competitive market.
Eg.: Ryanair, Inditex (Zara), etc.
4. Democratization of the market. Birth of a new disruptive technology that allows a large
number of customers to enter the market, usually for lower prices. E.g.: Ikea, Tata, etc.
5. Socialization market. When the business model enables poor people access to basic
services. Eg Grameen Bank and Grameen Danone Foods.

STRATEGY CAPSULE 4.1 (Grant Book)
Business Models for Complex Business Ecosystems: Google and Ryanair
Google: At the heart of Google's strategy is a business model whereby free search supports paid advertising—over two-thirds of the revenues of
Google's parent, Alphabet, are generated by advertising placed on Google's own websites and applications. However, Google's full business model
is more extensive. It includes the following:
• Using its advertising management capabilities and relationships with advertisers to manage advertising placements on other content providers'
websites (AdSense).
• Gathering huge quantities of user data that allow more precise targeting of advertising.
• Protecting the availability and data-gathering capabilities of Google's search products by providing its own web browser (Chrome) and operating
systems (Android, Chrome OS).
• Sustaining dominance of online advertising through launching competing products against rivals such as Apple, Facebook, and Microsoft.
Ryanair: At the core of Ryanair's strategy is the low-cost carrier business model developed by Southwest Airlines (see Figure 1.3 in Chapter 1).
However, this model has been extended by Ryanair to exploit multiple sources of revenue generated by a range of partners. Elements of the
Ryanair business model include the following:
• Extreme unbundling. In addition to paying for flight tickets, passengers are encouraged to pay for services such as seat assignments, checked
baggage, priority boarding, credit card fees, and inflight refreshments.
• Payments from airports and local government authorities (incentives to Ryanair to initiate and maintain specific routes).
• Commission on sales of partners' complementary products and services such as car hire, train and bus services, insurance, hotels, theater, and
sports tickets—also ticket sales for other airlines (e.g., Air Europa).
• Advertising on Ryanair website, travel magazine, and seat backs.
Sources: Allan Afuah, Business Model Innovation: Concepts, Analysis, and Cases (Routledge, 2014); Ryanair Holdings plc, Annual Report, 2017.

It is related to a key success factor.

It should translate into a higher return compared to their

structure.

framework and, by extension, the structure, conduct and performance of the market.

S4.5. Limitations of Industrial Analysis
1.
Static perspective
−Industries that are more dynamic and continuously changing are not well represented
2.
No interaction among competitors
−Actions and success of one industry player may depend on the actions of other players in
the industry
−Session 13 & 14: Game theory
3.
Industry influence competition, but competition influence industry
−Industry structure influences competition
−But: Competition also influences industry structure
4.
Difficulty of defining industry boundaries
−Assumption that industry boundaries are given and well defined
−Industry boundaries vary depending on our objectives
−Session 6: Segmentation
5.
Excessive emphasis on industry structure
−Assumes that industry structure is the main determinant of firms’ profits
−Firms’ success also depends on firm-level factors (e.g. resources and capabilities)
−Session 7 & 8: Resource-based view

S5. Case: US Airline
Identifying Key Success Factors by Profitability Modeling: Airlines
Profitability, as measured by operating income per available seat-mile (ASM), is
determined by three factors: yield, which is total operating revenues divided by the
number of revenue passenger miles (RPMs); load factor, which is the ratio of RPMs
to ASMs; and unit cost, which is total operating expenses divided by ASMs. Thus:

Some of the main determinants of each of these component ratios are the
following:
• Revenue/RPMs
• intensity of competition on routes flown
• effective yield management to permit quick price adjustment to
changing market conditions
• ability to attract business customers
• superior customer service.
• Load factor (RPMs/ASMs)
• competitiveness and flexibility of prices
• efficiency of route planning (e.g., through hub-and-spoke systems)
• building customer loyalty through quality of service, frequent-flier
programs
• matching airplane size to demand for individual flights.
• Expenses/ASMs
• wage rates and benefit levels
• fuel efficiency of aircraft
• productivity of employees (determined partly by their job flexibility)
• load factors
• level of administrative cost.

S8. RBV – Case: Harley Davidson
Potential threats (1/3)
▪The economy
−All of HD’s major market (US, Canada, Europe, and Japan) face an economic
outlook in which consumer discretionary expenditure is likely to be
constrained for many years
−Harley motorcycles = Expensive leisure item
−Less sales, when customers have less to spend
▪Demography
−Average customer age of 50 years old: Harley’s customer demographic is
much older than for the average motorcycle brand
−Problem: This demographic group (until recently swelled by the baby-boom
generation) is in declining
−But ‘older’ people might start to use motor cycles
▪Excess capacity
−Harley increased its capacity over the past two decades from 50,000 to
400,000 bikes a year
−A capacity that exceeds demand has several problems for Harley:
−
higher fixed cost base
−
a shortage of new Harleys helped maintain the second hand value of Harleys
−
the ubiquity of Harley bikes undermines the image of exclusivity
39
Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

S8. RBV – Case: Harley Davidson
Potential threats (2/3)
▪The appeal of the Harley image
−Preferences for lifestyle may change
−Will the macho, individualistic, leather-clad biker image be as popular in the
decade of the 2010-2019 as in 1990-1999?
▪Competition in core market
−Honda and the big motorcycle companies, all of which produce Harley-style
V-twin cruisers but typically with more advanced technologies and lower
prices
−Small producers (Excelsior, Polaris, Enfield, and Indian) producing retro-style
bikes
▪Competition in other markets
−Competition may come not just from other motorcycles but from other costly
‘toys’ (boats, other outdoor sports, and, ultimately, a wide range of leisure
pursuits)
−Competition also from:
−Stylish, high-performance sports bikes (e.g., Ducati, MotoGuzzi, Suzuki,
Triumph, Aprilia, and Kawasaki)
−Smooth-riding, highly engineered touring bikes sold by Honda and BMW

Potential threats (3/3)
▪The international market
−Appeal outside US may differ from the national market (Less nostalgia, about
the style style and values that HD motorcycles represent)
−How far Harley should adapt its products, its image, and dealership strategies
to national markets?
−Does Harley really understand its overseas markets?
▪Entrapment in a narrow niche market
−To what extent is Harley trapped within a narrow niche market (the US market

−Whenever Harley tried to expand outside its core market – either overseas or

−Growth prospects within its core market are limited

makes it different from the others, placing it in a superior
competitive position.

It must be relevant.
•
It must be sustainable over time.
•
It is related to a key success factor.
•
It should translate into a higher return compared to their
opponents or the potential to do so.

S9. Competitive Advantage
3. Cost Advantage vs. Differentiation
SEGMENTATION
SEGMENTATION: When the competitive advantage is only for a certain segment of the
market.
•
Segmentation in cost leadership. Cost leader for a small market segment.
Ex.: Decathlon basic prices for golf clubs
•
Differentiation segmentation. Find a niche where it competes with in an oligopoly
usually high prices are set.
Ex .: Painting for yachts.
DIFFERENTIATION VS. SEGMENTATION
•
Differentiation: Concerns choices of how a firm distinguishes its
offerings from those of its competitors →
How the company is going to differentiate?
•
Segmentation: Concerns choices of which customers, needs, localities a
firm targets → Which segment or niche of customers?
