S9. Competitive Advantage
4. Drivers of Cost Advantage
3. PRODUCTION TECHNIQUES
The correct design of processes and incorporating technology are two of the main catalysts
for the reduction of costs in organizations. There are three elements that favor:
1. Mechanization and automation of processes. The intensive use of machinery is able
to reduce costs in most processes and prevents operators from performing repetitive
activities of little value added. Ex .: automotive sector.
2. The efficient use of materials. Using technology supported by human knowledge is
achieved to maximize the materials and therefore reduce waste (time, materials, etc.)
3. Organizational accuracy. By production techniques the organization can adjust to
maximize the accuracy of organizational processes to avoid costs.
•
Just in time → Reduce financial costs and storage
•
Lean thinking → Reduces several types of costs (ex. Organization team)
•
Total quality / Six Sigmma → Reduces costs of poor quality.
•
Process reengineering (Hammer and Champy).
26
Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

S9. Competitive Advantage
4. Drivers of Cost Advantage
4. PRODUCT DESIGN
A well design product or service may reduce a lot of costs.
•
Facilitate automation. The way in which a product or providing a service that is
supported by automating processes within the design.
Ex .: The bottles and cans have at the base a recess to facilitate packaging mechanization.
•
Reduce the cost of materials. Through good product design can reduce the
consumption of materials, waste recycling system or material.
Ex. The cans have been reduced to half its thickness in the last 30 years, they are
recyclable aluminum and just wasted in their manufacture.
•
Assembly cost reduction. Design a product for simplifying assembly and
manufacturing process so that fewer resources are used for processing.
Ex .: The cars each assembly are made with fewer parts. It is the supplier who has to
deliver the semi-mounted.
27
Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

S9. Competitive Advantage
4. Drivers of Cost Advantage
5. INPUT COSTS
The cost of resources used to manufacture the products or services directly impacts the
cost.
•
Location advantages. The resources have close or that the cost of transporting or
using the input is reduced.
Ex.: Silicon Valley using Standford´s IT engineers; Ceramic Industry in Castellón using
Teruel´s clay.
•
Take ownership of low-cost inputs. Take ownership not only reduces the purchase
price for the lack of intermediaries, but also reduces the costs associated with
inefficiencies of coordination with outside companies.
•
Having a strong bargaining power. Used to force the price/quality ratio. Note that it
must be sustainable in the medium-long term.
•
Cooperation with suppliers or integration into the value chain.
28
Ricardo López Pérez, PhD, MBA Strategic Management

S9. Competitive Advantage
4. Drivers of Cost Advantage
6. CAPACITY UTILITATION
•
Increasing the production capacity to its maximum.
This cost reduction is the larger if the proportion of fixed costs/variable costs is high.
•
Reducing excess capacity.
•
Flexible resources to adapt quickly to changes in the environment.
•
Reducing installation costs. This reduces the barriers to entry and exit from the
sector.
7. RESIDUAL (ORGANIZATIONAL EFFICIENCY)
•
Organization Design. Reduce the corporate areas, flat
structures and avoid redundant areas.
•
Organizational laxity. Over time organizations create laxity
in costs. You are maintained over time out of habit or
convenience, but provide very little value to the company.
•
Organizational Culture and Leadership. Leader values such
as austerity or transmitted luxury corporate values and
therefore the organizational culture.
Ex. IKEA → Ingvar Kamprad.

•
TOP DOG: This strategy implies that the post-entry behavior of a company is aggressive, and there is a high
level of entry barriers in the market. The incumbent retaliates when it sees the entrance of a new player.
•
FAT CAT: This strategy implies that the post-entry behavior of a company is accommodating, and there is a
high level of entry barriers in the market. The incumbent does not retaliate when it sees the entrance of a new
player, as they know the entering competitor will also be accommodating.
•
LEAN & HUNGRY: This strategy implies that the post-entry behavior of a company is aggressive, and there is
a low level of entry barriers in the market. The incumbent retaliates when it sees the entrance of a new player.
This implies competition will increase in the market.
•
PUPPY DOG: This strategy implies that the post-entry behavior of a company is accommodating, and there is
a low level of entry barriers in the market. The incumbent does not retaliate when it sees the entrance of a
new player. This implies competition will not increase in the market
